Crude oil tankers, bulk carriers and vessels sit anchored near Qaboos Port in Muscat, Oman [File: Elke Scholiers / Getty]
Iran says that seven oil tankers have been struck and sustained damage in the Strait of Hormuz, the largest single-day toll for the waterway since the United States and Israel started their war against Iran on February 28.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said in a statement on Thursday that four of the vessels were transferring oil when they were targeted and caught fire overnight. The other three were disabled after striking mines.

list 2 of 3 Netanyahu promises Iran regime change: Can Israel topple Tehran government?
list 3 of 3 Rising costs and tight budgets strain Americans ahead of midterm elections
The claims could not be independently verified, and the report did not provide details about possible casualties or the tankers’ flags.
The IRGC also warned that it could strike US bases across the Middle East if Washington moves to help tankers transit other parts of the strait.
“The US military must know that if this trend continues, the conflict will extend to its bases in the region,” the IRGC said in a statement on its Sepah News website. “This is a serious warning.”
Iran claims control over Hormuz, a strategic shipping route through which one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies passed before war broke out. It regularly attacks ships that attempt to navigate the strait without its authorisation.
But the US military has been escorting vessels through the waterway in increasing numbers, with Iran responding by stepping up attacks.
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that “Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of oil prior to the US Midterm Election”.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, he added: “They are making up fake hits, mines, and everything else because more oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the conflict.”
A US Central Command spokesperson, speaking anonymously to Al Jazeera, also called Iran’s mine claims incorrect.
The spokesperson said US forces have cleared the international shipping lanes of mines and that Iran is using missiles and drones.
The strait remains open, the spokesperson said, with 95 percent of vessels getting through.
The attacks, the spokesperson added, show Tehran’s “desperation” under the US blockade, which cuts Iran off from the resources it needs to rebuild the military capabilities the US has said it destroyed.
“The number of ships and tankers attacked every single day is increasing, and Iran is saying it is continuing to do this because they are not going to allow any change in that situation,” said Al Jazeera’s Mohamed Vall, reporting from Tehran.
“They have full control over the Strait of Hormuz right now, they say.”
Vall said there is also talk in Tehran about an imminent escalation in the war, with the Iranians expecting the US to attack even before US midterm elections in early November.
“The IRGC army chief has boasted that Iran is more ready than anytime before, and has produced enough weapons and equipment to wage a symmetrical war against the United States,” he said.
Reporting from the US White House, Al Jazeera’s Kimberly Halkett said: “Striking Iran does not appear to serve any Republican interests”, adding that pre-election polls tell the same story for Trump’s political party.
“What we’ve seen in surveys in recent months, and as of today, is that most Americans want relief from their tax money going to pay for any potential war with Iran that is ramped up,” Halkett said.
“There is real frustration over the rising cost for everyday Americans, given the rising fuel prices that have occurred as a result of this conflict  … As a result, the US president is having to make the case.
“The pressure is on the president, and it’s not just from the opposition party,” she said. “It is also from within the Republican Party as well.”

items.title: Surveillance and 'constant paranoia': Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow
items.summary: Officials compare working in Russia since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine to the Cold War era.
items.content:
Image caption, Ex-US and French ambassadors Lynne Tracy and Pierre LÃ©vy were among those to speak to the BBC of their time in Moscow
"Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 and 2025, tells the BBC.
US, UK and European diplomats once played a crucial role in Russia, defusing tensions even at the worst moments of the Cold War.
But now, deemed "unfriendly" by President Vladimir Putin's government, Western ambassadors are under constant surveillance, isolated and increasingly cut off from the country they were sent to understand, as the war in Ukraine grinds on through its fifth year.
The BBC has spoken to five diplomats who have served in Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion.
They compare current pressure levels to the Cold War era - when Western embassies were monitored through physical surveillance, listening devices hidden inside gifts , and "spy dust" - a near invisible chemical agent used to track officials.
Hundreds of Russian diplomats were expelled from countries in Europe and the US after the war began in 2022. Moscow responded in kind, declaring hundreds of Western diplomats persona non grata and leaving many embassies short-staffed.
Tracy's 30-year career took her to countries like Pakistan, where she survived an armed attack in 2008. But she says that even under constant physical threat, her posting in Peshawar was, in a sense, easier than Russia.
"There, I still felt that there were things within my control. What made Moscow more difficult were the high levels of uncertainty."
The constant pressure from Russian counterintelligence was the primary source of such uncertainty, she recalls.
Image caption, Tracy pictured leaving Russia's Foreign Ministry after being summoned by Moscow in 2023
Russian diplomats in the West also complain of such unfair treatment. But according to the diplomats who spoke to the BBC, the scope and tactics of Moscow's intelligence services are far greater.
"Expect listening devices, expect cameras in every single room of your house," a former European diplomat says of the warning he received before leaving for Moscow.
Another ex-ambassador says they were forced to dismiss two Russian employees after Moscow's domestic security service, the FSB, tried to recruit them, demanding that they report on everything going on at the diplomatic mission.
The pair told the embassy instead, who let them go - "otherwise, they could have faced some sort of criminal prosecution".
Meanwhile, Russians who would ordinarily build relationships with diplomatic staff - such as those working in academia and culture - are also being intimidated into avoiding contact with Western officials.
One former ambassador says his guests were once "tailed" by FSB agents right up to the doors of the embassy.
Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
Europe targeted by spiralling campaign of sabotage - and Russia is the chief suspect
Just this June, guests invited to the British ambassador's residence in Moscow for the King's birthday celebrations said they had been harassed by pro-Kremlin activists and state-media journalists, and then questioned by the police.
One of the guests says he has since declined several invitations to events at Western embassies out of fear.
One former ambassador says "constant paranoia" has driven a number of officials to quit their jobs. Even after leaving Russia himself, he adds, he was looking over his shoulder for months.
'Generals prove what they can do in war. The same is true for diplomats'
In the immediate aftermath of the invasion, there were discussions across Europe about whether to recall ambassadors or stop working in Russia altogether, says former French ambassador Pierre LÃ©vy.
He remembers calling Paris immediately to say pulling their envoys would be a mistake, feeling that the worse relations became, the more important they would be.
The invasion quickly transformed their work, says another ex-European ambassador; the co-operation required for their usual efforts on bilateral relations, trade and joint projects was now impossible.
And for those who stayed in Russia, the war left them with a host of new priorities beyond supporting their own citizens and companies.
Firstly, countries viewed as unfriendly by Moscow still wanted at least some channel of communication with Russian officials to get an accurate picture of what was happening inside the country.
But they also had to protect their staff and keep their embassies functioning.
Image caption, Pierre LÃ©vy (second from the left) and Lynne Tracy (second from the right) pictured at the funeral service for opposition leader Alexei Navalny in March 2024
After Russia's ban on hiring foreign nationals in 2021, the US embassy's facilities team was left significantly understaffed. Ðven a minor plumbing issue like a leaking pipe could turn into a major problem, draining the time of diplomatic workers.
One diplomat recalls discussing staffing shortages with a Russian official, who advised him not to get too upset. "He said, 'at least you still have the chef'."
Financial sanctions imposed by Western governments to support Ukraine created different day-to-day difficulties. After Russian banks were cut off from the Swift payment network, and Mastercard and Visa suspended operations in Russia, many embassies struggled with basic operating expenses.
A former ambassador recalls simply running out of cash and being unable to pay his staff - until another diplomat, who was selling his car after being expelled, brought the rubles to the embassy in a suitcase.
"It's completely insane," the diplomat laughs. "But you had to look at it with a sense of humour."
Image caption, A wooden replica of the Great Seal of the US was given to the American ambassador to Russia as a gift in 1945 - it was later found to contain a listening device
Russian officials make little secret of their attitude towards Western diplomats. They have openly accused those from "unfriendly countries" of engaging in "espionage".
Moscow has been particularly critical of those who show an interest in expressions of dissent against the Kremlin and, according to Russian journalist Alexei Venediktov, has effectively banned most Russian officials from speaking to Western embassies.
This has only worsened relations with the West, says Venediktov, who recalls telling Russian officials: "You are being misunderstood precisely because of your own actions - because ambassadors cannot do their jobs."
Today, Moscow has little to no contact with many Western governments, says one ex-European ambassador. "There are no calls, no meetings at ministerial level."
But they say this has made diplomats all the more important, left with the responsibility to communicate their governments' positions to Moscow.
"Generals prove what they can do during a war. The same is true for diplomats. When things get really difficult, every single thing you do actually matters."
Lynne Tracy left Moscow in 2025 feeling she had accomplished her primary mission: the US Embassy had held firm.
But she is also proud of the work she and her team did to maintain connection between Americans and ordinary Russians.
"Because at some point, government-to-government relations will have a chance to improve - and those ties between people will be there to help speed the improvement."

Ukrainian officials have reported slow connectivity with Starlink, a key tool for their defence systems [Odd Andersen/AFP]
By Al Jazeera Staff , Reuters and The Associated Press
United States President Donald Trump has said that tech mogul Elon Musk has restored Ukraine’s access to Starlink, a satellite internet service that plays a key role in Kyiv’s war effort and air defences.
On Thursday, Trump declined to discuss a report from The Wall Street Journal that he had called Musk and instructed him to end restrictions on Ukraine’s connection.

list 2 of 3 ‘I don’t care how it’s done’: Trump pressures Ukraine to cut peace deal

The news outlet reported that Starlink services returned to normal following the call.
“I don’t want to comment on it, whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn’t make any difference, I guess. The bottom line, he put it back,” Trump told reporters when asked about the report.
On October 13, Ukrainian officials announced that sudden restrictions on Starlink services had left the country’s military scrambling.
Though the system came back online, connectivity has reportedly remained spotty.
Questions have persisted about where the decision to restrict access came from, with Musk and the Trump administration officials trading blame.
Trump has denied ordering restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starlink.
“Well, I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” he said on Friday. “And from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.”
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said this week that decisions about Starlink’s speed and access belong to Musk.
“The bottom line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how ⁠their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at,” Rubio said on Wednesday.
But Musk has denied any responsibility , stating that Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, is “owned and controlled by the US government”.
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he said in a social media post on October 14, using the acronym for “president of the United States”.
The Starlink speed caps and restrictions have also raised concerns that Trump, or the president’s right-wing allies, might seek to leverage such technology to pressure Ukraine into complying with US demands.
Trump has had a contentious relationship with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, repeatedly calling him “difficult” in comparison to his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin.
Ukraine has been locked in a slow-grinding war with Russia since February 2022, after Putin launched a full-scale invasion of the Eastern European country.
While Europe has backed Ukraine’s defence against the invasion, Trump has suggested Ukraine itself could be to blame for the conflict.
In 2025, for instance, Trump blamed Ukraine’s ambitions of joining NATO. “ I actually think that that was the thing that caused the start of the war,” he said at the time.
More recently, Trump posted on Truth Social that it was Zelenskyy’s fault the war had not yet ended. “He doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” Trump wrote.
As the war continues, Trump has been criticised by Democrats and some members of his own Republican Party for easing US pressure on Russia.
Recently, his administration issued a series of announcements to buy Russian diesel and ease restrictions on Russia’s energy sector.
Those decisions come as Trump is struggling with the political fallout of high fuel prices caused by his decision to join Israel in launching a war on Iran.
He has also suggested he would be open to a trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, which would be a first for the three leaders.

items.title: Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supply
items.summary: Iran’s IRGC says it hit four vessels in the northern Gulf and three more struck mines near the strait of HormuzShipping workers: how is the Middle East conflict affecting you?Oil prices jumped to a five-month high on Thursday after ​attacks in Saudi Arabia and hits to tankers in the strait of Hormuz threatened further disruption
items.content:
Vessels at the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman. Photograph: Reuters
Vessels at the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman. Photograph: Reuters
Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supply
Iran’s IRGC says it hit four vessels in the northern Gulf and three more struck mines near the strait of Hormuz
Shipping workers: how is the Middle East conflict affecting you?
Oil prices jumped to a five-month high on Thursday after ​attacks in Saudi Arabia and hits to tankers in the strait of Hormuz threatened further disruptions to the world’s crude supply.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by 3% to hit $112 a barrel for first time since 18 May.
Yemeni Houthis , who are aligned with Iran, hit several targets in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, with two people killed and eight more wounded in a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people killed in a drone attack on a Saudi oilfield.
Elsewhere the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four vessels involved in “illegal” oil transfers in the northern ​Gulf were hit and caught fire after being tracked by its forces on Wednesday.
It said three more vessels collided with mines west of the strait of Hormuz, and warned the US that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases.
A chart showing the Brent crude oil price The US has now ordered some diplomats and family members to leave their missions in Saudi Arabia, and it plans to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the Middle East, according to Reuters, which also reported that Saudi Aramco has instructed staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely.
Concern is growing that conflict in the region could escalate further, almost eight months after Tehran’s effective block on the strait of Hormuz triggered what many feared would bring the greatest energy supply disruption in the history of the market. In the first weeks after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran , oil surged past $100 a barrel and market observers predicted prices of up to $150 a barrel as flows through Hormuz came to a halt.
Oil peaked at $126 a barrel in April during the conflict and fell back below $100 in late May and then to lows of $71 at the start of July amid hopes of a ceasefire in the region. The price began to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart and fresh hostilities broke out in the Gulf .
However, data from Kpler has shown that oil exports from the Persian Gulf have now risen above their prewar levels, partly because of an increase in oil pumped overland through pipelines to the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman.
Global stocks wobbled on Thursday amid expectations of higher inflation and borrowing costs. The Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, fell by 1%, with the UK’s FTSE 100 down by 0.7%.
In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 index dropped 2.7%, while the South Korean Kospi fell 3.5%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index shed 3%.
Shares in American Airlines dropped almost 4% in pre-market trading after the company warned that high fuel costs would push it into a loss this year.
American Airlines abandoned its previous forecast that it might achieve a profit this year as it faced “historic fuel cost pressure”.

items.title: Trump says Musk has restored access to Ukraine's Starlink network
items.summary: Ukraine relies on Starlink for a range of military uses - its owner Elon Musk has repeatedly denied restricting access.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Trump says Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink internet access after row
Elon Musk has restored Ukraine's Starlink internet access, US President Donald Trump has said, after restrictions hampered Kyiv's armed forces.
Trump made the comments after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said connectivity to the military-grade Starshield network, which is provided by Musk's satellite-based Starlink system, had yet to be fully restored.
Musk previously denied he was behind the slowdown, which affects Ukraine's ability to use drones to attack Russian targets in Ukraine and protect itself from attacks.
Trump refused to be drawn on a report that he had called Musk to ask him to lift restrictions to the service, but said: "Bottom line, he put it back."
The Trump administration previously denied instructing Musk's company to restrict access.
The connectivity restrictions came as Trump put pressure on Zelensky to stop Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, which he has argued have caused prices to rise.
Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.
Image caption, A Ukrainian soldier using a Starlink satellite internet terminal which connects to thousands of SpaceX satellites
Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed.
The networks use 10,000 satellites in low Earth orbit to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and battlefields.
Modern warfare often relies on the use of high-speed internet to effectively operate drones.
Earlier on Thursday, Zelensky said the speed of the system used by Ukraine's military had still not been restored fully.
He told a news conference that the speed "has not been restored to 400 [km/h; 250mph] yet", adding: "We are working on it."
He continued: "I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so."
The Ukrainian president made the comments shortly before the Wall Street Journal , external reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink.
The US outlet reported that Trump told Musk he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped at around 160km/h, according to officials.
The speed limit made Ukraine's offensive drones and interceptors powerless against Russian attacks.
The journal reported that the system was working more normally on Thursday, shortly after their conversation.
BBC News has not confirmed the Wall Street Journal's report. It has also contacted the White House and SpaceX.
Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing on 14 October.
Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink which Ukraine uses for some of its operation. He said the system was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting the US military may therefore be behind the restrictions.
The White House has repeatedly said it did not order access to be restricted.

items.title: CoreWeave’s market confidence erodes as bond yields spike and stock sinks
items.summary: CoreWeave shares are down 36% in October, and the spreads in its credit default swaps are widening.
items.content:
CoreWeave’s market confidence erodes as bond yields spike, stock sinks
CoreWeave's stock is down 36% this month, and the spreads in its credit default swaps are widening.
The company's elevated bond yield is prompting investors to question what additional financing options are available.
"Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients this week, referring to AI bonds.
CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator appears after the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on March 28, 2025.
CoreWeave is facing a crisis of confidence on Wall Street that's playing out in real time among equity and bond investors.
With interest rates spiking and AI build-out concerns mounting, debt-heavy neoclouds like CoreWeave are being viewed by many market participants as the most vulnerable trade in the artificial intelligence space.
"Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, a credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients on Tuesday, referring broadly to corporate debt in tech. Keches highlighted the "speed at which AI vibes are shifting on a day-to-day basis."
CoreWeave, which went public in March of last year and reached a peak market cap of about $90 billion three months later, is now valued at roughly $31 billion, with its stock down 36% this month after plunging 10% on Thursday. Its unsecured debt, meanwhile, is sporting a yield of about 15%.
The spread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, is up 179% in the past year and 39% in October. It last stood at 1,145 basis points, or 11.45%.
The story is playing out across the neocloud sector. Shares of Nebius are down 33% this month, while IREN's stock is down 38%. In Australia, shares of data center operator NextDC plunged 40% on Wednesday after the company slashed its annual earnings forecast. Earlier this month, Australian data center company Firmus scrapped its planned initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions.
U.K. neocloud Nscale is now under the microscope as investors wait to see whether the Nvidia-backed company will go through with its IPO. The company filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange last month.
CoreWeave is the biggest of the pack, and is intimately tied to the U.S. AI market. Nvidia is its top institutional investor, with a stake of about 9%, according to FactSet. And more than two-thirds of CoreWeave's revenue last year came from Microsoft .
That's put a spotlight on CoreWeave's financials and its ability to remain viable. The company has about $20.7 billion in debt coming due through 2030 and another $14.9 billion thereafter, with the prospects of higher interest rates on future financing.
Sources on credit desks told CNBC that the high-yield debt market is effectively on hold until after the midterm elections in two weeks given ongoing concerns about the political pushback that data centers are facing. One source, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter, said fixed income investors "want permitting and regulatory requirements to be substantially resolved" before they commit financing.
"Given recent turbulence, pausing makes sense," Seth Meyer, global head of client portfolio management at Janus Henderson, said in an interview.
CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator, who co-founded the company in 2017 initially as a crypto-mining venture, sent a memo to employees on Thursday, which CNBC obtained, to try and tamp down concern. Intrator stressed that the company maintains a range of funding options.
"Our financing model combines infrastructure-backed borrowing, corporate debt, equity, and customer prepayments," Intrator wrote. He added that the company has "additional flexibility to raise equity over time as market conditions and our capital needs warrant."
CoreWeave had $5.5 billion of cash and equivalents at the end of the second quarter. The company is expected to report third-quarter results next month. Analysts expect negative free cash flow in the period to swell to $10.1 billion, the highest since the company started reporting quarterly financials, according to FactSet.
One issue being debated heading into the report is how much more capital CoreWeave needs to raise. Rob Oliver, a software analyst at Baird, is estimating roughly $30 billion in 2027.
"Earnings may address financing measures to shore up confidence," Oliver said in an interview. "But they wouldn't need that capital until the first quarter."
Another question is whether Nvidia will step in if necessary?
Nvidia, which supplies the graphics processing units that CoreWeave rents out, invested $2 billion in January for a 10% stake. The purchase price was $87.20 a share. The stock is now trading at $61.82 even after jumping 6% the day of the announcement.
While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said last week that CoreWeave doesn't need a backstop, some investors say the chip giant's further participation may be necessary if credit conditions continue to worsen.
Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Analysts at Goldman Sachs , JPMorgan Chase and Barclays have put out bullish notes on the company this week, highlighting the company's GPU-backed loans and its solid list of investment-grade customers like Microsoft and Meta . Goldman analysts emphasized the company's strength in the market relative to many of its neocloud competitors.
"Not all neoclouds are created equal," they wrote, in upgrading their rating to buy from hold. "CoreWeave is likely in the top quartile of neoclouds, if not the top decile, when measured on performance and ability to execute."
— CNBC's Michelle Fox and Jordan Novet contributed to this report.

Bond traders are backing off Fed rate hike bets — here's what it means for mortgage rates
If oil is about to spark an inflation wave, the bond market hasn't heard about it.
Brent crude ( BZ=F ) is trading around $112 a barrel, more than 50% higher than before the Iran war began in late February. Normally, that kind of spike would have bond investors worried about inflation and pushing interest rates higher.
Instead, Treasurys are rallying on Thursday as stocks slide. The 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ) is on track for its biggest one-day drop in more than two years, slipping back below 5%. When bond prices rise, yields fall. That matters for anyone shopping for a home, because mortgage rates tend to follow the 10-year .
Behind the move is a quick change of heart about the Federal Reserve as long-term interest rates decline. The Fed meets next week, on Oct. 28, and investors have been bracing for it to raise rates to fight perceived oil-driven inflation.
Those bets are fading fast. Fed funds futures now put the odds of an October hike at about 5%, according to Bloomberg data. That's down from 15% on Wednesday and 37% at the end of September.
The outlook for December has shifted too. As recently as Wednesday, traders were fully priced for a hike by year-end. Now they see roughly a 75% chance.
Bloomberg, Yahoo Finance Why bond traders aren't panicking about oil
Even with oil soaring, the bond market's inflation forecast has barely budged.
One way to measure what investors expect is the gap between regular Treasurys and Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, or TIPS , which pay extra when prices rise. That gap, called the breakeven rate , says investors expect inflation to average about 2.4% a year over the next five years. That's the same as before the war started.
So why did yields climb so much this year? Almost all of it came from "real" yields, which is what bonds pay after inflation. That's a bet the Fed will keep rates high enough to stop oil from turning into lasting inflation, not a bet that inflation is about to take off.
Bond yields soared on real rates, not inflation bets · Federal Reserve, Yahoo Finance Not everyone buys the market's calm. Bloomberg strategist Simon White argues breakevens are "mispricing" the oil shock.
The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate fell to 7.32% this week from 7.40%, according to Freddie Mac. That's the first drop in two months, after a seven-week climb that took rates to their highest level since 2023. Before the war, rates were just under 6%.
Freddie Mac's survey doesn't capture Thursday's bond rally. If yields stay lower, mortgage rates could follow in the coming days.
The damage from this fall's surge is already showing up. Pending home sales, which track signed contracts, fell to a record low in September , according to the National Association of Realtors. "Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates," said NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun.
Buyers who did sign are walking away. About 14.5% of homes fell out of contract in September, according to Redfin data. That's the highest share on record outside the early months of the pandemic.
The bond rally held up through Thursday afternoon's sale of five-year TIPS. Bloomberg strategist Cameron Crise saw a sign that some big investors were scrambling to unwind bets on higher rates.
The next big test is the Fed decision next Wednesday.

items.content:
Trump claims Iran is 'making up fake hits' on tankers to drive up oil costs ahead of elections
Trump accused Iran of fabricating reports of tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz to drive up oil prices ahead of the US midterm elections.
US President Donald Trump speaks to members of the media as he departs the White House en route to Iowa, in Washington, DC, US, October 22, 2026.
US President Donald Trump accused Iran of fabricating reports of attacks on oil tankers and naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz to drive up oil prices ahead of the November midterm elections in a Truth Social post on Thursday.
“Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the US Midterm Election ,” Trump wrote.
“They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict."
Trump also accused Iran's regime of killing protesters and reaffirmed his commitment that Iran would not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.
The post came as Trump continued to defend the US campaign against Iran and its impact on American energy prices ahead of the November 3 congressional elections.
US President Donald Trump arrives at a campaign rally in Sioux City, Iowa, US, October 22, 2026. (credit: REUTERS/Evan Vucci)
Speaking to reporters at the White House before departing for a campaign rally in Iowa on Thursday, Trump said the war had come at a political cost but maintained that preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon was necessary.
“There’s a price to pay, which I knew immediately when I did it,” Trump said. “But we can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Asked about public reaction to the war, Trump said Americans had mixed feelings about the campaign .
“In one way they love it because I’m doing what should have been done by other presidents. In another way, maybe they don’t,” he said.
Trump also suggested the US could carry out further military action against Iran, saying Washington had already inflicted significant damage but “may do it a little bit further.”
The Strait of Hormuz has remained a key point of contention during the conflict, as attacks on commercial shipping and restrictions on maritime traffic have threatened the flow of oil through the waterway.
Iran's IRGC Navy reported that four oil tankers were hit and caught fire overnight, according to the Iranian state media IRNA. The incidents added to concerns about a renewed escalation in the region and the potential effects on global energy supplies.
Trump, meanwhile, argued that oil was moving through the strait at a higher rate than before the war, despite what he described as fabricated reports of attacks.

items.summary: Markets tumble as concerns about Iran war and high AI spending collide  NBC News
items.content:
The U.S. and Israel are reportedly preparing to resume military strikes on Iran following the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Atta Kenare / AFP via Getty
Oct. 22, 2026, 11:09 AM EDT  /  Updated   Oct. 22, 2026, 4:12 PM EDT
U.S. equity markets sold off sharply Thursday, as fears that Israel and the U.S. would restart attacks against Iran sent oil prices higher and major tech stocks failed to hold on to recent gains.
The S&P 500 closed down 1.2%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 2.6%. The price of international Brent crude climbed nearly 4% to $113 a barrel, its highest level since May, while U.S. crude gained more than 2% to close at more than $99 a barrel.
Demand for Treasury bonds also increased — bucking the trend of the past several weeks — as investors sought out the safe-haven assets amid riskier ones like tech stocks selling off. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note fell below 5% for the first time since late September.
The market moves were sparked in part by reports that Israel and the U.S. were preparing for a military operation in Iran after the November midterm elections.
Likely targets include Iran’s energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, according to The New York Times .
U.S. military and diplomatic personnel were also being evacuated from several countries in the Middle East, NBC News reported.
Iranian officials have promised widespread retaliation to any strikes, pointing to critical Middle East data center sites and undersea internet cables as potential targets.
“It’s been another difficult 24 hours for markets, as investors grapple with AI growth concerns, higher oil prices, and ongoing fiscal stress,” Henry Allen, director and macro strategist at Deutsche Bank, wrote in a note to clients Thursday.
Major tech stocks led the declines in equity markets, with Meta and Tesla dropping after both companies reported quarterly earnings Wednesday.
Meta, led by Mark Zuckerberg, reported that a scarcity of computing power is hindering the expansion of its Muse personal assistant overseas. Annabelle Gordon / Bloomberg via Getty Meta’s earnings and revenues beat forecasts, but only after excluding billions of dollars in legal penalties the company paid last quarter. It also warned investors that it expects to increase its spending in the coming year to meet demands for computing power.
A separate regulatory filing revealed that Meta intends to spend an additional $825 billion on contracts related to its AI infrastructure build-out.
Tesla, meanwhile, said it was reining in its capital spending plans, disappointing investors who were hoping for a signal of more aggressive expansion.
Elon Musk's Tesla reported it was scaling up its Cybercab fleet in Austin, Texas. Win McNamee / Getty The slide in the Nasdaq got additional fuel Thursday after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in an appearance on CNBC that capital to finance the AI investment boom was becoming “scarce” due to higher interest rates and a glut of existing spending commitments.
Despite Thursday’s rout, the S&P 500 remains near the all-time highs it set earlier this month.

Stock market today: S&P 500, Nasdaq tanks as tech stocks sink amid AI trade worries, Meta shares plummet
Updated Thu, October 22, 2026 at 8:37 PM CDT 1 min read
US stocks fell on Thursday as the Tech ( XLK ) sector plummeted, with worries over the AI trade resurfacing following earnings from EV maker Tesla ( TSLA ) and social media giant Meta ( META ). Investors flocked to bonds, sending Treasury yields lower as oil prices surged to a five-month high .
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) was little changed, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell 1.2%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) tumbled 2.6% as semicondcutor stocks fell, reversing gains from Wednesday's session.
Neocloud provider CoreWeave ( CRWV ) sank 10% as worries over the cost of capital and its impact on debt-heavy balance sheets resurfaced.
Meanwhile, Meta shares tanked nearly 7% as investors weighed the company's quarterly results and 2-for-1 stock split announcement.
Tesla shares were volatile after an earnings beat , as investors weighed lower 2026 capex against higher spending in 2027 and 2028 on Optimus, Cybercab, and Terafab. SpaceX ( SPCX ) stock fell, giving back more than half of Wednesday's post-earnings gain.
Meanwhile, Blackstone's ( BX ) stock climbed 8% following the firm's upbeat outlook for upcoming investment sales after posting weaker third quarter earnings amid elevated borrowing costs.
A report that the US and Israel are preparing for renewed attacks on Iran after the US mid-term elections sent Brent crude ( BZ=F ) to $113 per barrel while West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) climbed to $100. A deadly attack at a Saudi Arabian airport and oil field also put upward pressure on energy prices.
In other news, jobless claims fell to 194,000 last week , the fewest in three months, underscoring how layoffs remain low.
Worries over AI spending and the cost of capital resurfaced on Thursday, sending semiconductor stocks and hyperscalers shares lower.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose just above the flat line, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) dropped 1.2%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) tumbled 2.6% with technology stocks taking the brunt of the beating.

Meta ( META ) stock plunged nearly 7% following its quarterly results and the announcement of a 2-for-1 stock split. EV maker Tesla ( TSLA ) ended the session lower by 3%, despite a better-than-expected quarter.
Moderna shares plunge on leaked vaccine study results
Shares in the pharmaceutical giant Moderna ( MRNA ) plunged on Thursday, falling by more than 20% after results from a new cancer vaccine study were leaked on social media.
The stock's fall put the company on pace for its worst daily performance since going public in December 2018.
Though the results for the new drug being developed by Moderna — the initial announcement of which sent shares surging by more than 100% — appeared strong, they weren't quite as high as investors were hoping , per The Wall Street Journal.
The trial vaccine is designed to prevent the spread or resurgence of melanoma, a form of skin cancer. The details of the study were expected to be publicly shared on Saturday at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference, per WSJ.
The results reportedly showed that the vaccine reduced the risk of the cancer spreading by 38% in patients with a high-risk form of melanoma versus standard treatment, according to TD Cowen analyst Tyler Van Buren.
Big companies are rethinking 'out of control' AI spending — and turning to cheaper models
IBM ( IBM ) is calling attention to a growing trend among companies and their AI spending: They're keeping a closer eye on it.
"I think what we are seeing is that at least larger enterprises are becoming a lot more cognizant and a lot more aware of what the true ROI of all of their AI spend is," IBM CEO Arvind Krishna said during the tech company's earnings call on Wednesday.
"They are also getting worried if some of the AI spending is completely out of control with no real return," he added.
Meta stock drops more than 6% despite strong Q3 results, stock split
Bitcoin ( BTC ) fell below $82,000 early Thursday as crypto joined a broader sell-off in riskier assets amid rising geopolitical tensions.
The world's largest cryptocurrency traded around $81,600 Thursday morning, down more than 3% for the last 24 hours. Other major coins also declined.
Crypto's total market value fell 1.4% over the previous 24 hours, according to CoinMarketCap. Traders saw roughly $400 million in liquidations over the same period, according to data aggregator CoinGlass.

The 10-year Treasury yield (^TNX) is on track for its biggest one-day drop in more than two years on Thursday, slipping back below 5% as stocks slide. The 5-year yield (^FVX) is falling even faster. Meanwhile, Brent crude (BZ=F) is hovering around $112, up more than 50% since the Iran war began in late February.
The surprise is how little the oil spike has moved the bond market's inflation forecasts.
The 5-year breakeven — the inflation rate implied by the gap between regular Treasurys and inflation-protected TIPS — is a bit lower now than it was before the war.
The 5y5y inflation swap is the market's forecast for average inflation over the five years starting five years from now, and the Fed watches it closely for signs that expectations are slipping. It has barely moved.
So the jump in yields since February has been almost all about real rates — not inflation. Traders are betting the Fed keeps policy tight enough that $110-plus oil doesn't turn into lasting inflation.
Not everyone buys it. Bloomberg strategist Simon White argues breakevens are "mispricing" the oil shock.
Elsewhere in bondland, France's 10-year yield is above the US 10-year for the first time since 2013.
Next up is the 5-year TIPS auction at 1 p.m. ET. Bloomberg's Alyce Andres calls it a referendum on the Fed's inflation bet under Chair Kevin Warsh. Weak demand would signal investors are starting to doubt it.

Treasury yields fell as investors flocked to bonds amid pressure on the AI trade.
The 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ), which moves inversely to bond prices, fell 11 basis points to 5.02%. The 30-year Treasury ( ^TYX ) yield also slid 10 basis points to 5.32%.
Concerns over a slowdown in AI infrastructure build-outs overshadowed inflation fears stemming from higher oil prices.
Blackstone stock climbs 4% as executives give upbeat Q4 exit outlook
Blackstone (BX) stock rose 4% Thursday morning, reversing earlier losses as executives at the alternative asset giant offered an upbeat outlook for investment exits and fee growth in the coming quarters.
Blackstone CFO Michael Chae told analysts that performance-fee realizations from investments already under contract and expected to close in the fourth quarter would surpass the firm's total net realizations in the third quarter. He also reiterated expectations for "double-digit" growth in base management fees in 2027.
The outlook offered investors some encouragement after Blackstone reported a 34% drop in net realizations during the third quarter compared with a year earlier while distributable earnings fell 9% in the same period.
CEO Stephen Schwarzman described the quarterly results as "strong" amid a "volatile external environment" in a statement accompanying the earnings release.

Chip bulls sprang a bear trap on Tuesday. Two sessions later, they're the ones getting caught.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) is down about 4% premarket, below Tuesday's intraday low of $489.70. That was the floor of the bear trap — a breakdown that quickly reverses, catching traders betting on further losses. SOXX is on track for its lowest close since July 29.
Lam Research ( LRCX ) is leading the slide, down about 9% after its results Wednesday night. Applied Materials ( AMAT ) and KLA ( KLAC ) are off about 6%, and AMD ( AMD ), Intel ( INTC ), and Sandisk ( SNDK ) are down 4% to 5%. Nvidia ( NVDA ) is off a milder 2%.
SOXX is on track to flip direction for a fifth straight session, and the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) for a seventh.
Dip buyers keep showing up anyway. Semiconductor ETFs saw record flows over the past week, Bloomberg senior ETF analyst Eric Balchunas posted Thursday. "Buying the dip here has [a] pretty good record of working," he wrote.
There's little room to hide. "Every index on the planet is basically an AI index," Manulife John Hancock Investments co-chief investment strategist Matt Miskin said on Yahoo Finance's live show Thursday.
Watch whether buyers come in yet again this session. A close above $490, roughly Tuesday's trap low, keeps the bulls' hopes alive — barely.
Oil prices rise to highest level since May on worries of Iran-US escalations after midterms
Oil prices rose on Thursday to their highest level since May amid growing worries over an escalation of the war in the Middle East after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Brent crude ( BZ=F ) topped $111 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) hovered above $98 a barrel.
The US and Israel have reportedly drawn up plans for renewed attacks on Iran after the elections next month, according to the New York Times , citing unnamed US officials.
Meanwhile, Middle East tensions escalated after Saudi Arabia said it suffered attacks at the airport of Dammam and an Aramco oil field .
Tesla reports Q3 earnings beat, positive free cash flow, and better-than-expected capex
Tesla ( TSLA ) reported better-than-expected third quarter earnings on Wednesday, with its free cash flow and capex spending coming in ahead of Wall Street estimates.
Tesla reported Q3 revenue of $28.05 billion vs. Bloomberg consensus of $28.13 billion. Tesla posted adjusted EPS of $0.48 vs. the $0.44 estimate, with adjusted EBITDA of $3.90 billion vs. $3.66 billion.
Tesla stock was volatile following the earnings release.

IBM shares slide as revenue outlook holds steady despite earnings beat
IBM ( IBM ) shares were volatile in pre-market trading on Thursday after the company beat Wall Street's top- and bottom-line estimates and raised its full-year free cash flow forecast, but maintained its 4%-5% revenue growth guidance for 2026.
Software revenue accelerated by 9%, but CFO Jim Kavanaugh said about a quarter of that growth came from closing "tens of slip deals" that were delayed from the second quarter.
This suggests third-quarter software growth was partly driven by delayed revenue rather than entirely by new demand.

The Latest Inflation Data Spells Bad News for Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the Stock Market
The U.S. Federal Reserve is tasked with keeping inflation under control, which typically means targeting an annual increase of around 2% in the Consumer Price Index (CPI). When inflation is too high, it puts pressure on household budgets and reduces corporate profit margins, so the Fed often hikes the federal funds rate (overnight interest rates) to put the brakes on the economy and cool prices down.
The CPI rose at an annualized rate of 3.4% in August, prompting the Fed to hike rates for the first time in three years at its September meeting. Fed chairman Kevin Warsh also warned more rate increases might be on the way if inflation remains persistently high, and the latest batch of data suggests that is exactly what is happening.

Rising interest rates can spell bad news for the stock market for a few reasons. In fact, the Fed's last rate-hiking cycle resulted in a bear-market decline of over 20% in the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) index. Here's what investors need to know.
Image source: Getty Images. Inflation is moving in the wrong direction
The U.S. and Iran have been locked in a fierce geopolitical conflict since late February. In an attempt to gain leverage, Iran has closed the Strait of Hormuz waterway, through which 25% of the world's seaborne oil transits each day. To make matters worse, the ongoing conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen took a turn for the worse recently, knocking even more oil supply offline.
As a result, a single barrel of West Texas Intermediate crude trades for over $100 as I write this (Oct. 19), a whopping 77% increase from its 2026 opening price of $57. Consumers now face soaring prices at the pump, but they are also paying more for groceries and retail products because it's suddenly more expensive to fuel the trucks, boats, and planes used to transport them.
The CPI increased at an accelerated annualized rate of 3.7% in September, with the energy component jumping by 20.4%. But it could get worse, because the September Producer Price Index (PPI) increased by 6.3%, with energy surging by 35.4%. The PPI measures the change in input costs for businesses, which are typically passed on to consumers through higher prices, so it's often a leading indicator of future CPI readings.
The CME Group 's FedWatch tool, which tracks the probability of interest rate moves by analyzing the 30-day Fed Funds Futures market, suggests there is a 91% chance of another 25 basis-point hike in December. It also predicts two more hikes in March and June 2027, so it seems Wall Street is betting that high inflation is here to stay.
Rising interest rates are bad news for the stock market
When interest rates rise, consumers are forced to allocate more of their household budgets to debt repayments, leaving less money for discretionary spending. Over a long enough period of time, this can put a dent in corporate earnings, and earnings typically drive stock prices.
High interest rates also make companies think twice about borrowing money to fund their expansion plans, so investors start pricing in slower sales and earnings growth, which often leads to lower stock prices. Better yields on risk-free alternatives like cash and government Treasury bonds only accelerates the shift away from stocks when the growth outlook is uncertain.
The Fed's last rate-hiking cycle spanned from March 2022 to August 2023, and the S&P 500 was down more than 20% at its lowest point during that period, officially placing it in a bear market.
It's impossible to predict how long the Fed's current hiking cycle will last, but the S&P 500 is especially vulnerable to a correction right now because of its valuation. It's trading at a Shiller Cyclically Adjusted Price-to-Earnings (CAPE) ratio of 41, the second-highest level behind only the peak of the dot-com bubble in the year 2000. In fact, the index's CAPE ratio is so high that it might still be expensive even after a bear-market decline of 20%.
As a result, investors should tread with caution right now, particularly if they are trading risky derivatives like options contracts, or using margin loans to amplify their returns. These practices can lead to substantial losses if volatility ramps up.
The best approach is to stay focused on the long term. History suggests the market tends to recover and set new highs given enough time, so using a potential dip to buy an S&P 500 index fund and consistently adding to the position could yield excellent results over a period of 10 years or more.

items.title: Iran threatens to strike oil and AI facilities across Gulf if US and Israel renew attacks - The Guardian
items.summary: Iran threatens to strike oil and AI facilities across Gulf if US and Israel renew attacks  The Guardian
items.content:
Mohsen Rezaei said there could be no arrangement in which Iran’s economy came under attack while the economic architecture enabling those attacks remained immune. Photograph: Mohammed Salem/Reuters
Mohsen Rezaei said there could be no arrangement in which Iran’s economy came under attack while the economic architecture enabling those attacks remained immune. Photograph: Mohammed Salem/Reuters
Iran threatens to strike oil and AI facilities across Gulf if US and Israel renew attacks
Iran’s security chiefs say there will be ‘zero red lines’ if Trump and Netanyahu attack again
Iran will strike oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities across as many as seven countries in the Gulf in the event of a fresh US-Israeli attack, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, has said.
Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Mohammad Ghalibaf, the hardliner who led Iran’s negotiations with the US to end the conflict between the two countries, said Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed in principle on an attack, but could not guarantee a successful outcome. He added: “We see the next conflict as an existential threat. The third war in two years means a threat to existence. Our strategy is ‘zero red lines’.”
Mohammadi said: “We break the temporal and spatial dimensions of the conflict. The war will continue longer and in a wider geographical area than the enemy anticipates.”
An Iranian actor wearing a Donald Trump mask poses inside a mock prison cell attached to a billboard in Tajrish Square in Tehran. Photograph: AFP/Getty Iran’s ability to mount such operations, including any unofficial help it receives from China or Russia, will be a key factor in any American decision to restart the war.
Iranian media reported that Rezaei had declared: “In the event of a war, cables, datacentres and artificial intelligence facilities could also be targeted. If the conflict breaks out again, we will have a broader plan.
Some US diplomats told to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
“There can be no arrangement in which Iran’s economic lifelines come under attack while the economic architecture enabling those attacks is considered untouched and immune.”
According to recent reports in US media, US military advisers have drawn up a detailed list of targets for a fresh joint US-Israel assault on Iran to be implemented after the US midterm elections on 3 November.
Foreign ministers from three European countries, as well as Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt, will meet in Istanbul on Friday to establish agreed policies on the linked Iranian, Yemini and Palestinian crises. There is alarm that a further war is now the working assumption in Tehran and Washington.
Pete Hegseth, Trump’s defence secretary, met Netanyahu on Monday in Israel to discuss the timing and purpose of a joint US-Israel attack. Photograph: Samuel Corum/Pool/CNP/Shutterstock The naval services of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) claimed to have simultaneously struck four commercial ships seeking to navigate through the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The ships were said to be transferring oil from ship to ship.
The IRGC claimed a further three ships had been struck when they hit mines in the strait. There was no independent verification that this number of ships were hit, but Brent crude oil was trading at $113.4 a barrel, a recent high, propelled by US reports of the imminent renewed joint Israeli-US assault on Iran.
Trump has backed away from striking Iran again seven times in the past four months. However, a deadlock in diplomatic negotiations has led US government officials to brief about a potential new military campaign that would target missile sites, oil installations and nuclear sites.
The sabre-rattling by both sides has coincided with extended joint-training manoeuvres by the US and Israel, including practice runs over Iraq. Dozens of Israeli planes also flew close to the Iranian border earlier this week, according to the news site Axios. A big fire at a large aluminium factory in Arak in central Iran suggests sabotage operations may be under way inside the country.
Iranians walk past an anti-US billboard depicting a member of Iran’s military placing a foot on a US unmanned underwater vehicle. Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPA Netanyahu met the US secretary of defence, Pete Hegseth , in Israel on Monday to discuss the timing and purpose of a joint attack, including the possible political implications for Netanyahu’s chances of re-election.
Netanyahu would prefer it if Iran attacked first, he reportedly told Hegseth.
A US military buildup is due to be completed by early November, before a possible newly Democrat-inclined Congress or Senate take their seats in January. Trump intends to have stationed three aircraft carriers, thousands of marines, fighter jets and special operations forces in the Middle East by November.
Reza Nasri, an international lawyer close to the Iranian foreign ministry, said: “A third wave of war would not stay contained. Power grids, desalination plants, refineries and ports across the region would burn. Tens of millions would be left without water or electricity, and a massive wave of refugees would move from Arab countries towards Europe.
Containers and debris float in the water after the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride sank near the strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman on 14 October. Composite: Reuters “Hormuz would close completely, oil would spike, and the global economy would tip into recession. Israel’s economy, already bled by mobilisation and missile fire, would not survive a prolonged war of attrition. And Trump would be trapped in a crisis that consumes the rest of his presidency and leaves a wreck for his successors,” Nasri said.
Fars news agency, which is close to the IRGC, said Iran had issued directives to its various military and operational units “stipulating that in the event of a new widespread war, involving the assassination of Iranian officials and the killing of civilians, the Iranian response will not be limited to military targets, but will also include political targets”.
Mediators from Iran and Pakistan this week again explored familiar if reconfigured options for a ceasefire, including proposals that Iran receive billions in frozen assets in return for lifting its blockade of the strait, allowing UN weapons inspectors to view its bombed nuclear sites and to export its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country.
Iran has offered to end the Hormuz blockade within seven days and start talks on its nuclear file, but only if preconditions are first met, including lifting US sanctions.

On the first anniversary of the Novi Sad tragedy people filled the streets. Photograph: Armin Durgut/AP
Friday briefing: How a leaderless student group is challenging power in Serbia
In today’s newsletter: ​Born from the fury surrounding the deadly Novi Sad station collapse, Serbia’s Student List has taken its protests all the way to the elections in an unprecedented grassroots campaign
Good morning. As waves of youth-led protests swell across Europe , prompted by the cost of living, unaffordable housing and education standards, in Serbia the younger generation is taking on the apparatus of the state itself.
In tight-run parliamentary elections this Sunday, the country’s most consequential political movement in decades, Student List, is challenging former Slobodan Milošević henchman Aleksandar Vučić and his 12-year domination of Serbian politics.
Two years on from a singular national tragedy that galvanised public anger at state cover-ups and corruption, gen Z have channelled their energy and fury into a bold experiment in direct democracy, creating a genuinely leaderless, grassroots movement that is firing up disaffected voters across the country.
I spoke to Julian Borger , our senior international correspondent, who has just returned from Belgrade, about their hopes of emulating the defeat of Vučić’s ally, Viktor Orbán, in neighbouring Hungary and the potential for a democratic domino through central Europe. But first, the headlines.
UK news | Every Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in new government guidance designed to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency.
Ukraine | Russia has carried out a massive “demonstrative” attack on Ukraine, bombarding Kyiv with ballistic missiles just hours after Vladimir Putin said he had agreed to resume trilateral negotiations.
UK politics | Nigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader.
Europe news | Emmanuel Macron has said “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days as France seeks to get a grip on civil unrest after some of its worst street violence in years.
Energy | Great Britain is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter as its reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply is forecast to deepen.
In depth: ‘The essence of our movement is direct democracy’
A large group of Student List supporters arrive in Belgrade after marching from several cities across Serbia. Photograph: Pierre Crom/Getty Images It was, one Serbian student told me, “the drop that overflowed the glass”. On 1 November 2024, the collapse of a concrete canopy at the railway station in Novi Sad, Serbia’s second largest city, killed 16 people. The youngest was a six-year-old girl, Sara Firic, who was sitting on a bench with her grandfather and older sister. The Serbian Times reported they were still holding hands when their bodies were dug out of the rubble.
In the aftermath of the disaster, student-led protests developed organically, with demonstrators blocking a nearby crossroads for the same number of minutes as lives lost. As details emerged of botched refurbishment work carried out in what critics described as a corrupt deal with a Chinese consortium, the anger mounted. Ongoing protests were brutally suppressed and Vučić himself branded demonstrators western-backed “terrorists”.
Two years later, that single tragedy has sparked a mass movement for accountability and inclusive democracy to counter the creeping authoritarianism of Vučić’s Serbian Progressive party (SNS).
“There was a deep well of public discontent, and the students were inspirational in keeping the protest movement going,” says Julian.
Vučić expected the protesters to dissipate – instead, the mounting pressure forced the president to resign and call a snap parliamentary election, as he endeavours to consolidate his 12 years in power in a Putin-inspired switch to become prime minister.
In response, the student movement is fielding a list of 250 candidates of its own, mainly locally respected academics but also actors, musicians and farmers, with each candidate approved by citizens’ assembly.
Some polling suggests that Student List is edging ahead; others that the SNS is consolidating support. Julian tells me he left Belgrade with the sense that anything could happen on Sunday.
How did a student network put together an election campaign?
The Serbian student I spoke to is buzzing ahead of Sunday’s vote: “We’re really excited,” he tells me over the phone from the Serbian capital. “We hope we win.” He is studying for a masters in dramatic arts at the University of Belgrade, and asks not to be named in accordance with the leader-less structure of his movement.
He talks me through the “big collective effort”, including collecting canvas data door to door, and the “A student in every village” programme targeting Vučić’s base of rural voters, all coordinated by democratic citizens’ assembly. The thinking is that a higher turnout of disaffected voters will favour Student List.
Julian encapsulates the Student List movement as “a bold democratic experiment”, and that is how my student describes it: “The essence of our movement is direct democracy. This collective effort is about making people feel part of the decision-making, not just spectators.”
When Julian joined Student List volunteers canvassing in the housing estates of Krnjača, a Belgrade suburb, they were met with overwhelmingly positive reactions – “the response was ‘bring it on’” – though he caveats that opinion in outlying suburbs varies from those of the urban intelligentsia and others in more rural settings.
“People were saying to the volunteers, ‘Take my contact and tell me anything I can do on election day.’ There’s a feeling of now or never.”
The demands of the student movement are focused on governance, Julian tells me, and their slogan, “Serbia or mafia?”, highlights repeated allegations of links between the SNS and organised crime, something the government denies. “Student List wants a rules-based order that conforms with the constitution on paper, not the system of classic crony capitalism that Vučić has established, where everything depends on your link to the SNS.”
Julian says Vučić is plainly taking the Student List threat seriously. He made 129 live television appearances in August, more than four times the previous month’s total.
But the elections are happening in a context of growing repression: Serbia has regressed in international rankings for press freedom and corruption in recent years. And only last week, the Guardian revealed that Vučić intervened to advance an allegedly illegal scheme to hand over a protected landmark in Belgrade for a Trump tower, another spur for recent protests.
A September survey for Serbian pro-democracy group the Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA) found no negative coverage of the ruling majority on the country’s television channels, compared with 37% of the time for the opposition.
Student List has accused the foreign ministry of rigging the diaspora vote by keeping overseas polling stations open where support for Vučić is strong, while closing them in parts of North America where the opposition could expect to perform well. The ministry did not respond to Julian’s request to comment.
Meanwhile the digital rights group SHARE Foundation found that members of the student movement had been targeted by advanced spyware, while Reuters this week reported on intimidation and beating of protesters by police.
What is the likely aftermath of Sunday’s elections?
With preliminary results expected in the early hours of Monday morning, a fundamental problem for the country is that neither side sees the other as legitimate, says Julian. “So in the aftermath of the election, barring a really clear decision, it will be disputed one way or another.”
Indeed, the European Council on Foreign Relations has warned of further street protests and possible violent repression, depending on the outcome and the margin of victory.
Big questions remain around how Student List would configure themselves as a government. Reforming the state and economy after more than a decade of highly centralised SNS control will be immensely challenging. So far their policy platform has been decided by full general assembly, and divisive issues such as future relations with Kosovo or Russia, and stance on EU membership, have been played down.
Although Serbia is an EU-candidate country, public opinion on accession is split, and the SNS has counter-balanced relationships with the US, Russia and China, particularly after the Trump administration opened dialogue on energy and technology with them earlier this year.
A Student List win would throw this geopolitical balancing act, which protesters argue brings little benefit to the people of Serbia, up in the air and potentially bring the country closer to Europe. And a contested Vučić victory would challenge the EU on whether to freeze diplomacy and funding to the country.
The student organiser I spoke with is clear that regime change is just the beginning: “Once we remove the regime, the big debate starts in Serbia about what we should do next. Should we join the EU? What about foreign policy? How are we going to democratise the country? There’s a lot that’s not working because of corruption. But right now we’re focused on these elections.”

items.title: Chip Stocks Fall as Supply Warning Deepens AI Selloff: Marvell and AMD Sink 8%, Intel Drops 7% - 24/7 Wall St.
items.summary: Chip Stocks Fall as Supply Warning Deepens AI Selloff: Marvell and AMD Sink 8%, Intel Drops 7%  24/7 Wall St.</f
items.content:
Chip Stocks Fall as Supply Warning Deepens AI Selloff: Marvell and AMD Sink 8%, Intel Drops 7%
A single comment from a chipmaking equipment supplier sent shockwaves through the semiconductor sector, and the companies most dependent on AI data center spending are paying the steepest price. Find out which chip giants are taking the hardest hits and…
Published October 22, 2026, 11:45am ET · 3 min read
The intricate architecture of a modern semiconductor chip, representing the advanced complexity in design that companies like Synopsys are mastering to drive technological innovation. © MF3d / Getty Images
A chipmaking equipment maker's supply warning is turning the artificial intelligence (AI) trade into a broad semiconductor selloff, and the chip designers most tied to data center spending are taking the heaviest hits. Marvell Technology ( NASDAQ:MRVL | MRVL Price Prediction ) stock is down 8% to $224.64 in morning trading, a drop that puts the custom chip designer at the front of the sector's retreat. Likewise, Advanced Micro Devices ( NASDAQ:AMD ) stock is down 8% to $509.79, matching Marvell's slide as one of the largest AI chip names gives back ground.
Across the group, the iShares Semiconductor ETF ( NASDAQ:SOXX ) is down 6%, a slide deep enough to show the damage spreading well past a handful of names. Intel ( NASDAQ:INTC ) stock is down 7% to $86.64, trailing Marvell and AMD while still falling faster than that sector fund.
Large-cap tech is holding up better, with the Invesco QQQ Trust ( NASDAQ:QQQ ) down 2%. That gap focuses the selling in chips and leaves the rest of the technology complex relatively steady, even after a rough stretch for the AI trade. Chip names are taking the brunt of a single comment from an equipment supplier.
The trigger came from Lam Research ( NASDAQ:LRCX ), which makes the equipment chipmakers use to build semiconductors. On its October 21 earnings call, Lam's chief financial officer, Doug Bettinger, stated that "this revenue guide would have been a bit higher if not for some near-term supply chain constraints that we are actively managing." Investors read that December-quarter comment as a sign that supply limits could hold back chip sales across the industry.
Tim Archer, Lam's chief executive, pointed to a longer runway for the bottleneck, saying: "As we move into calendar year 2027, we see clean room space availability and supply chain constraints for certain components continuing to limit chip makers and equipment companies' ability to fully meet end demand." Lam's management also stated that "The whole industry is going to have to work through very similar things," a line that extends the warning well beyond equipment makers. This latest wave of selling comes after a run of big technology earnings reports that put the AI trade under pressure.
Marvell and AMD Lead Losses as Selling Reaches Intel
AMD designs processors and graphics hardware for data centers and PCs, while Marvell develops custom chips and networking silicon for cloud providers. Among the chip designers most tied to data center AI spending, AMD and Marvell are also the stocks falling hardest. Marvell relies on manufacturing partners for fabrication, assembly, testing, and packaging, which links its results closely to outside capacity.
Intel both designs chips and manufactures them in its own factories. Having fabs hasn't spared Intel stock, which is still falling faster than the semiconductor fund, a sign the selling reaches chipmakers whatever their business model. Heavier spending on equipment, clean room space, and substrates is part of Intel's growth plan, and those inputs overlap with the bottlenecks Lam described.
Lam's own commentary offers a balance to the gloom around Marvell, AMD and Intel shares. Archer stated that "this is nothing like that" when comparing the current tightness with COVID-era shortages, adding, "I think we'll be caught up very shortly." Strong demand is what's straining suppliers in the first place, and Lam said some of its vendors are seeing orders from it grow even faster than Lam itself.
For Marvell, AMD and Intel, the question now is whether supply limits start showing up in their own outlooks. Bettinger expects shipments that slip out of the December quarter to go out in the March quarter, giving the market a concrete timeline for the bottleneck. Marvell's next outlook could show whether its data center momentum holds against tighter capacity.
For now, the semiconductor fund's steeper drop against large-cap tech keeps the pressure squarely on chipmakers. Investors should consider keeping their position sizes modest until the chip supply squeeze resolves.
