items.title: North Korea says it will resume propaganda broadcasts across border into South Korea
items.summary: North Korea plans to resume anti-Seoul propaganda broadcasts along the heavily armed border with South Korea, leader Kim Jong Un's sister said, reviving a psychological warfare campaign.
items.content:
North Korea says it will resume propaganda broadcasts into South Korea North Korea plans to resume anti-Seoul propaganda broadcasts along the heavily armed border with South Korea, leader Kim Jong Un's sister said, reviving a psychological warfare campaign.
North Korea says it will resume propaganda broadcasts across border into South Korea
FILE - A soldier stands at a North Korean military guard post next to loudspeakers, seen from Paju, South Korea, near the border with North Korea, on Feb. 26, 2026.
SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea plans to resume anti-Seoul propaganda broadcasts along the heavily armed border with South Korea, leader Kim Jong Un's sister said, reviving a psychological warfare campaign as tensions rise after land mine blasts injured three South Korean front-line soldiers.
Kim Yo Jong, her brother's top spokesperson on Washington and Seoul, made the announcement Wednesday after visiting front-line areas where North Korean troops are reinforcing the border. She renewed a threat to retaliate against any South Korean provocation aimed at the fortification work.
South Korea ditches 'denuclearization-first' strategy. What will Pyongyang do next?
In a follow-up statement Thursday, she said the North would place "new counter means" on alert along the border and have its loudspeakers on "standby" within days.
North Korea has been adding mines, barbed wire fences, anti-tank barriers and other fortifications to what's already one of the world's most heavily armed borders as Kim Jong Un pushes a hard line toward Seoul.
Touring the area with Marshal Pak Jong Chon, one of her brother's top military officials, Kim Yo Jong called the fortification work a "sacred and great undertaking" supporting the leader's policy of permanently severing ties with South Korea, which he has declared his most hostile adversary amid a broader diplomatic stalemate with Washington.
In this photo provided Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, by the North Korean government, Kim Yo Jong, center left, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, visits frontline areas, with military officials, in North Korea Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. Independent journalists were not given access to cover the event depicted in this image distributed by the North Korean government. The content of this image is as provided and cannot be independently verified.
"Our tactical hunting teams are taking new positions, and within October, the loudspeakers for psychological warfare against the ROK will be in operation along the whole border," Kim Yo Jong said, using the initials of South Korea's formal name, the Republic of Korea.
She warned that if South Korean warning shots — which Seoul says are meant to force North Korean soldiers doing fortification work back across the border — cause "actual harm to our territorial security and our service persons' safety," North Korean border guards "will show no mercy for the armed gangsters bereft of reason."
Asked about Kim Yo Jong's threat to resume the loudspeaker broadcasts, South Korean Defense Ministry spokesperson Chung Binna said Thursday that Seoul would need to take "proportionate measures" in response to the North's moves along the border, but did not elaborate on what steps are being considered.
North Korea's state-run Korean Central News Agency first reported Kim's border visit as Tuesday, but Kim later corrected it to early Wednesday in a separate statement.
Following an inspection with the U.S.-led United Nations Command, Seoul formally blamed North Korean-planted mines for the Sept. 21 border blasts and urged the North to apologize and clear its remaining mines. North Korea denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of strong retaliation if provoked.
"Our military leadership underlined the need to make those rogues aware that our new firepower units have taken their firing positions," Kim told soldiers during her visit Wednesday, reminding them of her brother's order to make the border with the "enemy ... eternally impregnable."
South Korea's military has said North Korean soldiers crossed the border's military demarcation line 50 times this year during fortification work, and that it responded with warning shots and broadcasts. Kim has said South Korean's claims of border crossings are a "false pretext," and that its provocations have increased "beyond the red line" since the mine blasts.
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff chairman, Jin Yong-Sung, called Kim's threats "intolerable" and ordered the military to "sternly respond" to potential provocations by the North.
During Tuesday's border inspection, Pak accused the South of making "deliberate, premeditated and absurd" claims to shift blame over the rising tensions and threatened an "overwhelming response" to South Korean provocations. He also denied that the North Korean soldiers were breaching the border during fortification work, saying "our army knows where our borderline is better than any others," KCNA said.
South Korea's new president turns off loudspeakers at the border with North Korea
Loudspeaker broadcasts are among the Cold War-era psychological warfare tactics the two Koreas have occasionally used against each other during times of tensions.
South Korea's liberal government, led by President Lee Jae Myung, halted its broadcasts after taking office last year to improve ties with the North, which later stopped its own.
Kim Jong Un in recent years has cut off all diplomacy and cooperation with South Korea and declared it a permanent enemy as a yearslong stalemate in nuclear negotiations with Washington drags on.

items.title: Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax
items.summary: The Meta boss had said he would exit the state over a wealth tax that has not yet come into force.
items.content:
Image caption, Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg
By Dearbail Jordan ,Â  Business reporter Â  and Â  Kali Hays ,Â  Technology reporter
Meta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires.
The agreement gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn (Â£149bn), even more shares in Meta to make up for the fraction of his fortune he may lose if the tax wins voter approval in November.
The measure would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents with a net worth of more than $1bn. It would likely see the Facebook co-founder pay around $10bn in additional state taxes.
He secured the deal with a special committee of Meta after "robust" and "at several points, contentious" negotiations, according to a Wednesday financial disclosure.
California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group.
The wealth of such people, including Zuckerberg, has ballooned in recent years. Meanwhile, his estimated effective tax rate in California was less than 1% , external each year.
Nevertheless, Zuckerberg told Meta's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California, and even selling his property in the state. His main homes in Californa are in Palo Alto and Lake Tahoe.
Such a move "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees", Zuckerberg told the board.
It would also "raise questions for management of the company going forward", he claimed.
In response, Meta decided to create more shares of stock in the company in order to give Zuckerberg a way to essentially make up any wealth he may lose through the tax proposal.
Through what's known as a stock split announced by the company on Wednesday , Meta created an entirely new type of stock and gave one new share to each existing shareholder. Zuckerberg is one of the company's largest shareholders and famously controls the company through the design of his holdings.
Through the deal, he will receive more stock, more often, and also be able to sell it on a quarterly basis, according to the company's financial filing. The shares will not change his level control over Meta, but they will allow him to cash in more easily on the company's value.
The deal appears to be effective even if the one-time tax in California does not pass, and will go on for eight years - as long as Zuckerberg remains a resident of California.
Meta called the deal with Zuckerberg its "Founder Alignment Agreement," saying it was "critically important" to keep him leading the company from California given the "dramatic and unprecedented transformation taking place in the tech industry and global economy related to artificial intelligence."
The company alluded to problems the company experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg began working outside of the office and mostly from his large compound in Kauai, Hawaii.
After a surge in hiring at Meta during the pandemic, a whistleblower scandal that led to renewed focus on child safety, and a refocus within the company to building out the "metaverse," which included renaming the company Meta from Facebook, the company began mass layoffs and restructuring.
Layoffs have continued into this year. The company's headcount is down 15% from a year ago, meaning it has shed at least 10,000 workers.
Today, the company has moved away from the "metaverse," or virtual platforms, and is more focused on artificial intelligence products and related tools.
With Zuckerberg leading the company's efforts to catch up in the AI race, Meta's board said it sees a future of "tremendous market opportunity" for the company.
Major tech companies are set to spend an estimated $1 trillion , external this year alone developing AI and the costly infrastructure around it, like data centres .
Meta said on Wednesday it planned to spend as much as $145bn this year on AI projects. The company has increased the amount it expects to spend on AI each financial quarter so far this year.
It is spending so much on the technology that it posted negative cash flow for the first time since the company went public 14 years ago. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Meta is now spending more money than it is bringing in.
And the company intends to spend even more in the year ahead. Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, said on Wednesday that another benefit of the stock split would be to give the company more ways to finance future spending on AI work.
The degree of the company's spending on AI, without an clear new revenue stream coming from it, appeared to spook investors on Thursday.
Meta's shares fell more than 7%, wiping more than $100bn off of the company's market capitalisation, a key metric used worldwide to measure the value of a publicly-traded company.
Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy

A snowy London street. Great Britain has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on production from the North Sea. Photograph: Shomos Uddin/Getty Images
A snowy London street. Great Britain has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on production from the North Sea. Photograph: Shomos Uddin/Getty Images
Some of Europe’s highest energy costs expected in Britain this winter
Official forecasts show country will meet energy demand by paying high prices to secure imports
Great Britain is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter as its reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply is forecast to deepen.
Energy system operators have said the country will have enough gas and electricity to meet demand over the coldest months – in part because of paying higher market prices than neighbouring markets to secure imports.
The official winter energy forecasts were published days after Europe’s gas market benchmark climbed to its highest level since December 2022 when Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sent prices rocketing.
National Gas, which runs Great Britain’s gas networks, set out its forecasts after striking an 11th-hour deal with the owner of a major Belgian pipeline to keep gas flowing into the country this winter by reversing a planned capacity cut.
The energy regulator, Ofgem, approved the deal – which will add around 10p a month to the average gas bill. Without the intervention there was a danger of gas running out in the event of a worst-case scenario where an important part of the country’s gas networks failed as temperatures plummeted.
In addition to gas imports by pipelines, Great Britain is expected to increase imports of seaborne liquified natural gas (LNG) cargoes by about 5% from last winter, according to National Gas forecasts, at a time when market prices are three times higher than they were before the Middle East crisis severely disrupted Gulf supplies.
Its winter outlook report suggested that prices could remain elevated if UK gas buyers need to compete more fiercely with countries in Europe for LNG cargoes amid low gas storage levels across the continent.
Europe ended August on course to enter the cooler months with gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years owing to the slowdown in gas exports from Qatar, one of Europe’s biggest suppliers, and the increase in gas consumption over the summer to power refrigeration and cooling during the record heatwaves caused by the global climate crisis.
The UK has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on homegrown production from the North Sea. UK production was forecast to fall by 6% this year compared with last winter, but the government’s controversial decision to approve the new Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea earlier this week, which was not fully accounted for in the winter forecasts, is expected to offer a modest boost to supplies when it starts up next month.
Great Britain is also forecast to be a net importer of electricity over the colder months, according to the National Energy System Operator (Neso) separate outlook report. That is also likely to come at a higher cost owing to tighter European power supplies compared with last winter.
The summer heatwaves reduced river levels across Europe, in a blow to French nuclear output and Norway’s hydroelectric reserves, which have remained below the 10-year minimum since late July.
The UK paid a record £4bn on power imports over the year ending in August, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics this week, of which half was spent on electricity imported from France. It has also made near-record payments over the past year to fire up gas plants while wind and solar farms have been paid to turn off due to bottlenecks in the grid.
Even though Great Britain will use gas power plants less overall this winter compared with previous winters thanks to rising renewable energy levels, the need for gas to play a role during power supply crunches could be 7% higher than previously assumed.
National Gas lifted its gas power demand forecasts for the most extreme electricity supply scenarios – when demand is unusually high and renewable output slumps – after noting over successive winters that gas plants have remained in high use when dark, still winter days lead to high electricity demand and lower renewable energy levels.
Glenn Bryn-Jacobsen, a director at National Gas, said: “While supply diversity and flexibility remain sources of resilience, taken together these trends in demand and supply have resulted in tighter supply margins during periods of high demand and system stress.”

items.title: Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 22, 2026 - Institute for the Study of War
items.summary: Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 22, 2026  Institute for the Study of War
items.content:
Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 22, 2026
The Kremlin's seeming interest in negotiations aims not to end the war in Ukraine but rather to secure economic concessions from the United States such that Russia can continue funding its war. Various Russian officials tried to present the October 21 meeting between US Special Representative to the Middle East Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin as evidence that Russia is willing to engage in meaningful negotiations to end the war while simultaneously attempting to extract economic concessions from the United States so that Russia can continue funding the war.[1] Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) CEO Kirill Dmitriev, for example, claimed on October 21 that Witkoff and Putin used the October 21 meeting to agree to expand Russian-US economic cooperation and to “continue communicating.”[2] A Kremlin domestic policy official told Russian opposition source Verstka that the Kremlin does not expect negotiations to resolve the war in Ukraine but that Russian officials hope to extract economic concessions, which could boost Russia’s budget and give Russia a military advantage.[3]
Other Russian officials meanwhile demonstrated Russia’s unwillingness to make any meaningful concessions toward ending the war in Ukraine. Kremlin Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov stated on October 22 that Putin did not present any Russian peace proposal to Witkoff during their meeting and that Putin has not considered the composition of a potential Russian delegation for a future Russia-US-Ukraine trilateral meeting.[4] Russian State Duma deputies expressed skepticism on October 21 and 22 that negotiations could end the war and reiterated claims that freezing the current frontlines would be detrimental to Russia's own efforts to end the war.[5] A source close to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) told Verstka on October 22 that the Kremlin has been working for over 1.5 years to try to sway the Trump administration to Russia's side and that the Kremlin's current negotiation efforts are emphasizing Ukraine's alleged hopelessness. These are similar to the Kremlin's earlier negotiation tactics which tried to convince the United States and the West generally that Ukrainian defenses were going to collapse such that Ukraine should preemptively capitulate.[6]
The Kremlin is fundamentally interested only in buying time to resolve the war on the battlefield while Russia simultaneously reaps the benefits of economic cooperation with the United States. State Duma Defense Committee First Deputy Chairperson Alexei Zhuravlyov stated on October 21 that Russia must "press" Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on the battlefield and force Ukraine to "capitulate."[7] Zhuravlyov added that Russia should not rely on diplomacy with the United States because Russian "successes on the ground” will strengthen Russia’s negotiating position.[8] Russian Presidential Aide Yuriy Ushakov similarly claimed that Russian forces maintain the "complete strategic initiative” and are conducting a "relentless offensive” in all key areas of the frontline.[9]
Russian forces are not winning on the battlefield, however, particularly as Ukrainian forces have stymied the planned Russian offensive to seize Donetsk Oblast. ISW has observed evidence that Russian forces suffered a net loss of 241 square kilometers of territory in Ukraine since September 1, 2026. The average rate of daily Russian advances has significantly declined since 2025, with an average of 0.25 square kilometers per day so far in 2026. Ukrainian forces have, comparatively, been contesting and seizing the operational initiative across several sectors of the frontline throughout 2026, including most recently in the Lyman direction with Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi which liberated over 270 square kilometers of territory and thwarted the Russian military command’s plan to encircle the Fortress Belt.[10] Russian forces are also facing mounting monthly casualties while the Russian recruitment rate continues to fall short of its loss rate.[11] Russian forces have suffered almost 37,000 casualties thus far in October 2026 — much higher than the 31,270 casualties for all of October 2025.[12] The Kremlin may face mounting challenges in the coming months, should Ukraine continue to contest the operational initiative and disrupt Russian offensive plans, potentially further pushing Russian commanders to urge Putin to conduct a mobilization in some form.[13]
The Kremlin is likely actively seeking economic cooperation with the United States as Russia faces significant financial strain. Sources familiar with the matter told Bloomberg on October 22 that even a few more months of continued war could exact lasting financial damage on Russian state-owned oil company Rosneft, as Ukrainian strikes against Rosneft's oil refineries have significantly reduced the company's profits and increased its debt.[14] Bloomberg added that repeated Ukrainian strikes have prevented Rosneft from completing repairs and restarting refinery operations and that strikes against complex secondary units that often include Western-sourced parts, like catalytic crackers, reformers, and hydrocrackers, are particularly difficult to repair. Russia remains highly susceptible to international sanctions that restrict its access to the technologically advanced components needed to repair the equipment damaged after Ukraine’s strikes.[15] The Kremlin is therefore pushing the United States for various forms of economic relief, so that Russia can continue funding its war against Ukraine.[16] The Kremlin has continuously sought to extract economic concessions during negotiations to alleviate the pressure on its oil industry — including restrictions on Ukrainian strikes against refineries and the relaxation of US sanctions against diesel exports — while expressing little real interest in ending the war.[17]
Russian forces conducted a massive missile and drone strike against Ukraine overnight on October 21 to 22 following the October 21 meeting between Witkoff and Putin — a continuation of Russia’s pattern of launching large strike packages in the days before and after major peace talks. The Ukrainian Air Force reported that Russian forces conducted a massive combined missile and drone strike primarily targeting Kyiv City and using an unspecified number of Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles and 210 long-range drones, 110 of which were jet-powered.[18] Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Russian forces conducted three waves of ballistic missile strikes against Kyiv City using 21 missiles, damaging residential, energy, railway, and commercial infrastructure.[19] Zelensky stated that Russian strikes targeted 12 Ukrainian oblasts, killing at least two people and injuring at least 34 people. Russian forces regularly conduct massive strikes in the days right before and after bilateral and trilateral talks, such as the August 2025 US-Russia Alaska summit, the November 2025 US-Ukraine talks in Geneva, the November 2025 US-Russia talks in Moscow, the December 2025 US-Ukrainian-European and US-Russian talks, and the January-February 2026 US-Ukrainian-Russian talks in Abu Dhabi.[20]
Russian forces struck Kyiv City with cluster munitions to purposely harm the civilian population, likely as part of wider Russian efforts to distract from Ukraine’s recent battlefield successes and ultimately force Ukraine into capitulation by making daily life untenable. Zelensky stated that Russian forces struck Pechersk Raion, the historic center of Kyiv City, with three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads that have a dispersion diameter of 400 meters.[21] The strikes damaged monastery buildings and other civilian infrastructure near the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra and the Holy Presentation Monastery. items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Share Iran reveals ‘offensive’ doctrine, US issues alert: Is war imminent? on social media
A police officer monitors traffic as he stands under portraits of Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei in Tehran on October 21, 2026 [AFP]
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says renewed attacks by the United States could prompt Tehran to invade neighbouring countries and hit bases used in US military operations as part of its new “offensive” strategy.
The warning on Wednesday came amid escalating attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a global energy chokepoint, and uncertainty over diplomatic efforts to end the nearly eight-month war.
list of 3 items list 1 of 3 US envoy Barrack defends decision to join Israel in war on Iran
list 2 of 3 Why the war on Iran could backfire on US regime-change goals
list 3 of 3 Why do the US midterms matter for Trump and Congress?
“Our defence doctrine was previously defensive; we used to say that if a country attacks us, we will respond. Now we say that if a country attacks us, we will both respond and launch an offensive,” IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebi said.
Washington ordered some diplomatic personnel to leave Saudi Arabia amid attacks from Yemen’s Houthis while US President Donald Trump has signalled that a decision on the conflict could come soon.
According to media reports, the US and Israel are planning potential attacks on Iran in the coming weeks.
As negotiations seem stalled and both sides exchange threats, could the region be heading towards another military escalation?
The IRGC on Wednesday announced a shift towards an “offensive and asymmetrical” defence doctrine, threatening to invade countries that launch attacks against it.
Mohebi said Tehran would no longer limit its military operations to retaliatory strikes.
Mohebi stressed that Iran’s missile stockpile has increased 1.5 times since the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025. He did not provide specific figures.
“The quality of the missiles has improved significantly, and their range, destructive power and accuracy in hitting targets have increased,” the spokesman said.
Moreover, Mohebi said Iranian forces were in the “stage of preparing to unveil the ‘father of all bombs’. This is something new for the enemy.”
Meanwhile, attacks in the Strait of Hormuz continued unabated.
The IRGC’s navy said on Thursday that four vessels it accused of being involved in illegal oil transfers were struck and caught fire in the northern Gulf. Three other vessels hit mines west of the strait, it added.
Before the war, one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz. While shipments through the strait are still below those levels, oil shipments from the region returned to pre-war levels last month as exporters found alternative ways to ship out their oil and gas, including using pipelines.
However, a flurry of recent attacks in the key waterway and the fighting between Yemen’s Houthis and its Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, which has resulted in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, have once again sent oil prices surging. Brent crude climbed above $110 a barrel on Thursday amid fears of further disruptions to regional energy supplies.
Iran’s shift towards an offensive military doctrine reflects Tehran’s determination to make future US-Israeli attacks significantly more costly, according to analysts.
Negar Mortazavi, senior fellow at the Centre for International Policy, told Al Jazeera that Tehran was drawing lessons from the wars of 2025 and 2026 after its previous strategy of retaliation failed to prevent repeated attacks.
“Tehran now wants to establish a new equation: Any future attack on Iran will come at a much higher cost for the aggressors,” she told Al Jazeera.
Unable to match conventional US military capabilities, Iran is increasingly relying on asymmetric warfare, including missiles, drones and its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, Mortazavi explained.
She said Tehran was pursuing a broader strategy aimed at imposing military, economic and political costs on Washington, including potentially influencing the November 3 US midterm elections.
(Al Jazeera) “Iran wants to teach Washington a lesson: Attacking Iran comes with a high price, one that can even cost elections,” Mortazavi said, referring to US surveys that are predicting electoral losses for Trump’s Republican Party.
She added that Iranian officials were closely monitoring the elections, believing the economic fallout from the war could damage the Republican Party’s prospects of retaining control of Congress.
“The long-term objective is to establish deterrence so that future American administrations think twice before daring to attack Iran again,” she said.
Political analyst Rami Khouri said the doctrine was also intended to ensure that the consequences of attacks extend to the US, Israel and regional countries supporting their military operations.
“That’s one part of the strategy, that the suffering and the damage have to be equal and reciprocal,” Khouri, nonresident senior fellow at the Arab Center, told Al Jazeera.
Khouri argued that Tehran was also seeking to challenge what it views as longstanding Western domination of the region.
“The Iranians are actually working to try to end the colonial period,” he said.
He added that Iran’s strategy could extend the economic consequences of conflict far beyond the Middle East, affecting energy supplies, transportation, insurance costs and shipments of essential goods.
“The pain is going to go way beyond just the Middle East and Israel and the US and will hurt people in other parts of the world,” Khouri said.
Trump has offered conflicting signals about Washington’s next steps.
On Wednesday, he said the US was no longer negotiating with Tehran and suggested developments were imminent. “We are going to have something one way or the other that’ll happen fairly soon,” he told reporters.
He also said Washington could end the war immediately but wanted a lasting outcome. “It’ll end very soon. We could leave now, but we want to make sure it lasts for a long time,” Trump said at a campaign rally in South Carolina.
Trump previously pledged not to attack Iran before the November 3 elections.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this week that reaching a peace agreement is extremely difficult and insisted that Iran must stop targeting commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
In recent weeks, Iran’s enrichment of uranium has re-emerged as a point of contention .
Rubio has maintained that Washington will reject any agreement allowing Iran to develop nuclear weapons, which require highly enriched uranium. “The United States will not support any deal that creates a pathway for Iran to ever have a nuclear weapon,” he said on Wednesday.
Tehran insisted its right to enrichment is guaranteed under the Non-Proliferation Treaty.
Iran has offered a seven-day plan to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for Washington ending its blockade of Iranian ports, easing sanctions and unfreezing Iranian assets.
Meanwhile, the US Department of State on Wednesday ordered nonemergency personnel and their families to leave Saudi Arabia after recent Houthi attacks.
The US embassy in Riyadh has warned of further attacks while American officials told the Reuters news agency that family members could be withdrawn from other Gulf missions.
State Department spokesman Tommy Piggott said departure orders for mission personnel across the Gulf have not been ordered, saying the current orders were for “employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only”.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reiterated on Sunday his pledge to topple Iran’s government, saying it was key to preventing it from rebuilding its nuclear programme and the “axis of resistance”, further raising prospects of an escalation.
Netanyahu made the comments as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister is locked in a tough battle to remain in power in Tuesday’s elections.
Analysts warned that renewed US-Israeli attacks on Iran are increasingly possible with both sides preparing for another confrontation despite the continued possibility of diplomacy.
“Another round of war seems to be approaching,” Mortazavi said.
“Both sides appear to be preparing for renewed confrontation while escalating tensions in the Strait of Hormuz increase the risk of a wider conflict,” she said.
Mortazavi added that the elections in the next two weeks in the US and Israel could influence the timing of military action but warned that the current trajectory appeared to favour escalation over negotiations.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, on Wednesday said, “Everyone must know that any action against Iran comes at a cost.”
“If diplomacy can create this understanding, we prefer diplomacy, but if the war continues, Iran has the necessary means to sustain its response,” Rezaei said, according to the IRNA news agency.
Echoing Mortazavi, Khouri warned that another confrontation could be approaching although he said US threats might still be part of a negotiating strategy.
“I think imminent conflict is on the cards, but I don’t know if war is the right word to use,” Khouri told Al Jazeera.
He said renewed strikes could target Iran’s critical infrastructure, including electricity networks, transportation systems, bridges and essential services.
“We’re probably going to get some severe attacks on a few targets that will try to make life in Iran very difficult,” he said.
However, Khouri cautioned that Iran’s ability to withstand another major military offensive while inflicting comparable damage on its adversaries remained uncertain.
“It’s not clear if Iran has the ability to withstand major new assaults against it,” he said, while stressing that Tehran was unlikely to surrender to military pressure.

Meta stock sinks nearly 7% as AI spend pushes free cash flow negative
Meta stock sank almost 7% Thursday as free cash flow turned negative and the company raised the floor of its expected capex spend.
Prices for the social media giant's five-year credit default swaps reached all-time highs.
Meta also revealed it would create a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg tries on Orion AR glasses at the Meta Connect annual event at the company's headquarters in Menlo Park, California, U.S., September 25, 2024.
Meta shares slumped nearly 7% on Thursday as the social media giant showed negative free cash flow in its third-quarter earnings and raised the floor of its full-year capital expenditures.
The spread on the social media giant's five-year credit default swaps reached all-time highs on Thursday, a signal of growing credit concerns from investors as the company leans deeper into its artificial intelligence spending plans.
Meta said it expects its full-year capex to range from $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from a previous $130 billion.
Free cash flow came in at a negative $2.12 billion during the quarter.
The company revealed Wednesday that it would create a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock during its earnings release, meant to maintain its "founder-led structure" and "provide Meta the ability to finance its growth."
Meta also said CEO Mark Zuckerberg could leave the state if the "California Wealth Tax" were to pass, as he "could become liable for a significant, multi-billion-dollar tax payment based on his ownership of stock in the Company," according to the SEC filing.
Zuckerberg was convinced to stay in California with the company's new stock plan, the filing noted.
Revenue for the social media giant jumped 26% in the third quarter from a year ago, coming in at $64.60 billion versus the $63.37 billion analysts expected. Earnings per share were reported at $3.83, though it wasn't clear if it was directly comparable with the $5.75 per share Wall Street was looking for.
— CNBC's Jonathan Vanian and Seema Mody contributed to this report.

items.title: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, History Says Investors Who Do This 1 Thing Always Win Out - The Motley Fool
items.summary: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, History Says Investors Who Do This 1 Thing Always Win Out  The Motley Fool
items.content:
The stock market has been shaky lately, with the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -1.21% ) , Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -2.60% ) , and Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI +0.02% ) all slipping from their all-time highs earlier this year.
Investors are feeling the uncertainty, too. The Fear and Greed Index measures investor sentiment on a scale from 0 to 100, with lower numbers indicating greater fear. In early May, the index peaked at 71 -- firmly in the "greed" category. As of this writing, it sits at 28, indicating fearful investor sentiment.
In other words, if you're feeling nervous about the market right now, you're in good company. Fortunately, history says one simple, proven strategy can help protect your investments right now.
If you're worried about a market crash, it can be tempting to sell your investments now before prices plunge. While that strategy may sound safer, it can be costly.
The market's short-term performance will always be unpredictable to an extent. When the market stumbles, it's impossible to know whether it's just a short-term fluctuation or the beginning of a crash.
For example, earlier this year, the S&P 500 plunged amid fears that the war in Iran would drag the market into a recession. Almost immediately, though, it rebounded. As of this writing, the index is up more than 13% so far this year.
While it may sound counterintuitive, history shows that the single best way to avoid losing money during a downturn is to continue investing consistently. When stock prices plunge, your portfolio may lose value . But you won't actually lock in losses unless you sell your investments for less than you paid for them.
For example, say you sold your stocks in March of this year, expecting the market to fall further. In that case, you'd have been hit twice: first by selling at discounted prices, and second by having to pay higher prices to reinvest later after the market rebounded.
Timing the market accurately is nearly impossible, and it can often cost you more than you gain.
The market has a flawless track record of long-term growth
Decades' worth of history proves that staying invested for the long term is the most lucrative way to build wealth in the stock market -- even when the short term is volatile.
During the dot-com bubble burst in the early 2000s, for instance, the S&P 500 sank by nearly 50% as the tech sector imploded. It took years for the index to reach a new all-time high, and shortly after it did, the Great Recession began in 2007 -- becoming the most severe economic downturn post-WWII.
Despite all of this volatility, however, the S&P 500 has soared by more than 750% since January 2000. In other words, if you'd invested $10,000 in an S&P 500 index fund or ETF back then and didn't contribute another dollar, you'd have more than $85,000 by today.
Along with a long-term outlook, it's equally important to invest in quality stocks. Not all companies will recover from a market crash or recession, especially if they're built on shaky foundations. During the dot-com bubble, for instance, many tech stocks surged despite weak finances or unsustainable business models. When the bubble popped, those stocks fared the worst.
No matter what may come this year or beyond, healthy stocks are best positioned for long-term growth. The right investments can help avoid losses during a downturn while setting you up for lucrative gains, too.

items.content:
Saab Q3 earnings: Fighter jet maker beats expectations as orders triple
Swedish defense giant Saab on Friday reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and sales, while orders trippled.
New orders came in at 65.8 billion Swedish kronor, up from 20.9 billion kronor a year earlier.
"The growing customer demand is reflected in major contract awards, including Gripen for Ukraine, GlobalEye and an order related to Germany's new frigates," CEO Micael Johansson said.
Swedish defense giant Saab reported better-than-expected third-quarter earnings and revenue on Friday, as new orders more than tripled from a year earlier, boosted by a deal to supply Gripen fighter jets to Ukraine.
New orders came in at 65.8 billion Swedish kronor ($6.6 billion), up from 20.9 billion kronor a year earlier, beating FactSet expectations of 56.4 billion kronor.
Third-quarter sales reached 20.6 billion kronor, ahead of FactSet expectations of 20 billion kronor. Earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) came in at 1.95 billion kronor, also beating forecasts of 1.9 billion kronor.
The results come as European governments race to turn defense spending pledges into military capability.
Saab's order intake included a 24.6 billion kronor contract for 16 Gripen E fighter jets for Ukraine, signed in June and booked in the third quarter. Deliveries are scheduled for 2029-2030.
"The growing customer demand is reflected in major contract awards, including Gripen for Ukraine, GlobalEye and an order related to Germany's new frigates," CEO Micael Johansson said in a statement.
Orders booked in the quarter also include a 10.1 billion kronor order for its military surveillance aircraft GlobalEye to an undisclosed customer in the Middle East, and an 8.7 billion kronor order for systems for German frigates.
Saab, whose products range from Gripen fighter jets and submarines to missiles and advanced electronics, has seen exponential order growth since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
Even with an ever-growing order book , booming sales, and increasing profitability, Saab stock, like many of its peers, has taken a hit in recent months as some investors question whether valuations have run ahead of the industry's ability to deliver.

items.title: Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC finds
items.summary: The UN human rights chief Volker Türk says the multiple attacks may amount to war crimes.
items.content:
Image caption, Medics at el-Fasher's Saudi Hospital performed a Caesarean by phone light on the day it was bombed
By Barbara Plett Usher ,Â  Africa correspondent Â  and Â  Mohamed Madi
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.
UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.
The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.
Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.
Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.
The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.
"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.
"The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned."
The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military.
Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities.
In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility.
But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query.
UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city.
The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city.
Reports of mass killings in Sudan have echoes of its dark past
Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say
Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023.
Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city.
Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies.
The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher.
In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city.
The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman.
The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says.
On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added.
The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist.
But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office.
They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs.
"There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners.
Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead.
"They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me."
That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said.
The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated.
Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base.
According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy".
In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim.
He also showed us what he called maps of landmines planted around the Teaching Hospital, which is located next to Sudanese military headquarters.
Doctors told us the hospital was not incorporated into the base and said they visited it to pick up medical equipment during the war.
The BBC has found no independent evidence of Dr Nugud's allegations. And the government of the Darfur region categorically rejected the charges.
After the South Hospital shut, its staff and remaining equipment were moved to the Saudi Maternity Hospital in the west of the city, where the army had its main bases.
Within days the pace of attacks on the facility picked up. At this stage the medical charity MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res (MSF) sounded the alarm.
"We do not know if hospitals are being intentionally targeted, butâ¦ the belligerents are not taking any precautions to spare them," it said in a statement.
However, in the course of our investigation we spoke to six doctors who described a pattern of systematic targeting.
They told us how Saudi Hospital was repeatedly struck - on some days up to 25 times, with a mix of shelling and drones, the latter "intelligent rockets" with precision-guided attacks.
Smaller medical facilities also came under fire. The BBC's timeline records the steady closure of private hospitals and neighbourhood clinics.
Furthermore, when some of these healthcare buildings shifted locations, the alternate venues were also attacked.
The Specialised Children's Hospital, which shut down at the beginning of the war along with the Teaching Hospital, moved to two other locations, both of which were then shelled and forced to close.
Similarly, the main dialysis centre was struck and then attacked again after it relocated.
By the time the RSF seized the city in October 2025, the Saudi Hospital was the only functioning health facility left.
The medical staff there had rallied to try to keep working as conditions worsened.
Doctors described how sandbags were set up to protect the building.
They built underground bunkers out of steel containers and established a number of alternative sites to house and receive patients and conduct surgery as the threat of attacks and the damage to the main structure steadily increased.
Dr Asow said this makeshift surgery was attacked five times in 2025.
In one case, he says, he was operating on a patient's neck when the building was shaken by an explosion - the medical staff ran out in fear, but he stayed.
In another case, health workers had prepared the theatre for an operation, but he told them to move the patient elsewhere because it needed a deep clean given the relentless case load. Shortly afterward the room was destroyed by shells - and the patient survived.
"From that day, some of my staff called me 'Mr Deep Cleaning' because they think that the issue of deep cleaning saved that patient," he said.
Dr Asow also describes how drones tracked the movement of patients.
On 15 March 2025, people carrying the injured from the site of an attack to one of the temporary wards were followed by a hunting drone, he says.
It struck as they reached the gate of the building, killing nine people.
On 17 August of the same year a donkey cart was transferring patients to the alternative operating theatre because all the ambulances had been destroyed, Dr Asow told the BBC.
It was hit by a drone, killing two patients, the driver and the donkey, he says.
Image caption, The burnt-out ruins of a building in a compound that housed a medical warehouse and dialysis centre in el-Fasher pictured after it was hit by a missile
The RSF health minister dismissed these accounts as "a continuation of lies" by the military (SAF) and their local allies, known as the Joint Forces.
"Even the medics, and many of the people who were there, because of this conflict, these tribal issues, these racial issues, they are allied with the Joint Forces and with the SAF. That's why you don't depend on that narrative," he said.
Doctors told the BBC they believed RSF fighters deliberately targeted medical facilities because army or allied fighters were among their patients.
The onslaught of shelling and bombing culminated on 25 October 2025 with the RSF storming the hospital amid allegations of a massacre that killed more than 460 patients and their companions .
The RSF has denied a massacre occurred, although the WHO condemned the reported killings and satellite imagery appeared to show clusters of bodies on the blood-soaked grounds of the hospital.
The BBC shared details of its investigation with the UN human rights chief, who said our findings were "deeply disturbing", and consistent with the analysis of his office.
"Our monitoring and documentation shows the RSF repeatedly struck el-Fasher's main hospitals and makeshift health facilities, destroying or seriously damaging them and severely impacting access to health services for thousands of civilians trapped in the city," TÃ¼rk said.
Healthcare in el-Fasher is now being run by the RSF-backed government. It has released several videos showing the Saudi Hospital and the Teaching Hospital re-opened, cleaned up and seeing some patients.
Dr Nugud says South Hospital is also set to reopen. He denied that doctors were forcibly abducted, telling the BBC that instead they had chosen to stay on to work.
"I have a video in front of the children's hospital when we freed a consultant, a doctor and six of the medical staff who were working with the SAF, and then when el-Fasher got liberated, there was a forgiveness for all of them.
The BBC spoke to one of the doctors in the video, Dr Al-Haj Mohamed Ahmed. He told us he had no choice: "I was forced to be there.
"If I spoke out of line, they'd put a bullet through my head."
He was among several medical workers captured while trying to escape the city and sent back, along with Dr Mustafa Ahmed.
They distinguished themselves by bringing a cholera epidemic in a temporary prison at the paediatric hospital under control and were subsequently taken to Saudi Hospital.
"They started to say that you are the people of the city, and we take the city, so we need to work together for the sake of the city," says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, who describes waking up several mornings in a row at the prison to find 50 inmates dead of cholera.
A year on from the fall of el-Fasher, the trauma of this dark period in Sudan's civil war is still painfully sharp.
The front lines have shifted elsewhere with no signs of a resolution to the conflict. And attacks on healthcare continue as part of a wider and devastating humanitarian crisis.

Kinder Morgan takes FID on Southeast Connector, Permian Link natural gas pipelines
The two pipelines would add a total of 5.4 bcfd of capacity starting second-half 2030. KMI's Q3 2026 net income grew nearly 22% year-on-year.
Map from Kinder Morgan Inc., October 2026 investor presentation.
Kinder Morgan Inc. (KMI) has taken final investment decision (FID) on its Southeast Connector and Permian Link natural gas pipeline projects. Southern Natural Gas (SNG), a KMI subsidiary, secured sufficient long-term, take-or-pay transportation agreements with shippers to proceed with Southeast Connector, designed to transport up to 2.6 bcfd through about 470 miles of new pipeline.
Subject to receipt of required permits and approvals, service is expected to begin in phases starting fourth-quarter 2030. The $3.1-billion project could be expanded if demand warrants.
"Large-load interconnection requests across the Southeast now exceed 200 Gw," said KMI chief executive officer and director Kimberly Dang in the company's earnings call, noting that this could represent roughly 8 bcfd of natural gas demand if it all came to fruition and if it was all served by gas-fired generation.
Natural Gas Pipeline Co. of America (NGPL), another KMI subsidiary, reached FID on the 2.8-bcfd Permian Link. Estimated cost of the project is $4.2-billion, of which KMI's share is expected to be about $1.6 billion.
The 434-mile pipeline will serve new power generation for an A-rated hyperscaler and is supported by long-term, take-or-pay transportation agreements. NGPL expects to place the project in service third-quarter 2030, subject to required permits and approvals.
KMI also sanctioned the second and third phases of its Creekside Lateral project in central Texas, following execution of additional long-term, take-or-pay agreements with data center and industrial customers. The company has now contracted 750 MMcfd of the system's 1.3-bcfd design capacity, with potential for future expansion to more than 2 bcfd. KMI expects to place the project in service in phases, beginning fourth-quarter 2026 and continuing throught fourth-quarter 2027, subject to permits and approvals.
SNG and Tennessee Gas Pipeline (TGP), meanwhile, took FID on the 10-bcf Bear Creek Storage Expansion project, to be used by TGP which has secured long-term binding agreements for the capacity. The extra capacity is expected to enter service in April 2029, subject to required permits and approvals.
KMI's Houston Ship Channel refined products hub moved 427,000 b/d across its 11 docks in third-quarter 2026, a 39% year-on-year increase and an all-time record for the site. The company attributed the record quarter to the worldwide shortage in refined product supplies and associated price dislocations and is advancing enhancements to in-tank blending capabilities for butane and other gasoline components.
Permitting and right-of-way acquisition also are progressing for two dedicated refined products pipelines connecting KMI's Pasadena Terminal with a nearby major refinery. The $139-million project is backed by a long-term storage and volume commitment with a major national oil company and is expected to enter service third-quarter 2027.
KMI is also expanding its 1.5-million-bbl Kinder Morgan Export Terminal on the Houston Ship Channel. The $30-million project is supported by a long-term storage commitment with a major international trading company and is expected to be placed in service first-quarter 2027.
The announcements and project updates were part of KMI's third-quarter 2026 earnings reporting. The company reported net income attributable to KMI of $764 million, up nearly 22% from third-quarter 2025.

items.content:
Nasdaq & Chip Stocks Plunge: Jensen Huang’s Stock Touting Fails as Market Delivers Heavy Blow to AI Bulls
The Nasdaq and chip stocks plunged, Jensen Huang's stock touting failed to work, and the market dealt a heavy blow to AI bulls.
In October 2024, U.S. AI chip stocks plummeted collectively, institutional investors reduced their holdings while retail investors bought the dip.
"There is little possibility of memory surplus before 2029."
On October 21 local time, Jensen Huang expressed his full support for the memory industry and backed the demand of the memory sector in a media interview during the GTC conference in Berlin.
This move to reassure the upstream industry is not a new practice. At Computex 26, Jensen Huang publicly stated that "Marvell is the next company with a market value of one trillion US dollars". Right after that, Marvell's share price closed up 32.25% in the trading session on June 2, marking the largest single-day increase in the company's history.
However, the market does not seem to buy this statement this time.
On October 22, Thursday of the US stock market, the NASDAQ Composite Index fell by 2.6%, posting the largest single-day drop since June; the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped by about 6.72%. Chip stocks including NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Micron, TSMC all slumped collectively, and Meta's share price also fell by nearly 7%.
From upstream equipment vendors, memory manufacturers, wafer fabs to Fabless design companies, and further downstream computing power customers and model developers, no stock has avoided a decline.
This pullback did not happen without any warning. Data from Goldman Sachs' prime brokerage division shows that semiconductor stocks have kept falling for consecutive days in the past week, and hedge funds have accelerated the reduction of their holdings in tech stocks. In this process, retail investors are still buying stocks related to chips, storage and AI cloud computing.
In contrast, Michael Burry, the prototype of "The Big Short", has shifted most of his short option positions to put options on the Nasdaq 100 Index and semiconductor ETFs. Another well-known short seller Jim Chanos has targeted new cloud computing companies that build data centers with borrowed funds and lease out AI computing power.
At present, the market is using changes in share prices to test risks in different links including the valuation of chip stocks, the supply and demand of computing power, and the financing cost of AI infrastructure.
On October 22 local time, the concentrated sell-off of US tech stocks once again put the market's concerns about the return on AI investment on the table. The direct trigger was Meta's quarterly performance report: affected by a substantial increase in capital expenditure, its free cash flow turned negative to 2.12 billion US dollars.
At the same time, the situation in the Middle East pushed up oil prices, adding new uncertainties to the outlook for inflation and interest rates. When financing costs and operating costs are facing upward pressure, the market's tolerance for large-scale capital expenditure of tech companies is also declining. Investors will inevitably ask when these aggressive investments can be converted into sufficient revenue and profits.
However, this is not a sudden adjustment. By October 16, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had fallen for eight consecutive trading days, with a cumulative decline of more than 15%. The pullback of semiconductor stocks started earlier than the concentrated sell-off on October 22, and the previous strong trading momentum of the AI industrial chain has loosened.
Griffin, the founder of Citadel, clearly emphasized in an interview with foreign media on October 20 that investors "are almost certain that there is an AI bubble".
He used the aviation industry as a metaphor to question how long the computing power price can be maintained after the GPU supply increases. He said: "GPUs, like airlines, have extremely low marginal operating costs. If we reach a point where GPU supply exceeds demand, marginal pricing will actually free fall."
On the corporate expenditure side, Griffin mentioned: "The entire US business community is looking at the bills from Anthropic and OpenAI and saying, 'Okay, we need to figure out how to make sure we get productivity gains from this.' But he does not deny the long-term value: "The companies on the other side of the bubble will be the market leaders for decades to come."
Griffin's judgment echoes the drop in chip stocks on October 22.
In this round of "violent pullback" of tech stocks, the market is not only worried about whether AI demand will grow, but also about whether the demand growth can support the current chip prices, computing power lease prices and valuations of related companies. In other words, when the invested funds can be earned back, and whether it can be earned back faster.
Michael Burry has long been emphasizing the bubble. He believes that the market may hit a major top in the next nine months, and warns that the rise in the final stage of the bull market may be more drastic.
In the drastic market pullback, institutional investors are the group that moves the fastest.
Data from Goldman Sachs' prime brokerage division shows that in the five trading days ending October 15, the speed at which hedge funds reduced their holdings in tech stocks reached the fastest level in at least ten years, and semiconductor stocks are one of the sectors with the largest reduction amount. Of course, this data only represents the transactions of customers covered by Goldman Sachs' prime brokerage business, and does not represent all positions of the entire hedge fund industry.
Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou, a strategist at JPMorgan Chase, also pointed out in the capital flow analysis that the performance of semiconductor stocks is correlated with the risk exposure of equity long-short funds. When related stocks start to fall, funds constrained by risk limits may further reduce their positions, thus amplifying selling pressure.
The investment blogger @aleabitoreddit known as the "White-haired Stock God" recently shared his position situation. He said the market is experiencing a large number of forced liquidations and panic selling. He has still obtained considerable returns since the beginning of this year, but some of his positions have pulled back recently.
@aleabitoreddit did not disclose the specific loss amount, nor did he say he encountered liquidation. This post presents the real feeling of individual investors in the market adjustment: even if there is still profit for the whole year, short-term pullback is hard to avoid.
Apart from the spot market, leveraged trading around chip stocks has also started concentrated liquidation.
CoinDesk cited data from CoinGlass that during the US stock market holiday on October 17, about 51.6 million US dollars of forced liquidation occurred in 10 minutes on cryptocurrency perpetual contracts linked to chip stocks and semiconductor ETFs, of which about 38 million US dollars came from long positions betting on price rise.
Specifically, the forced liquidation amount of SOXL-related contracts tracking triple long semiconductor stocks is about 12.7 million US dollars; positions related to Sandisk and SK Hynix each had about 10.8 million US dollars of positions forced to liquidate.
During the US stock market holiday on October 17, about 51.6 million US dollars of positions on chip stock-linked cryptocurrency perpetual contracts were forced to liquidate in 10 minutes, with long positions accounting for 38 million US dollars.
@davidyjeong, CEO of trading firm Tread.fi, analyzed the order flow at that time on X. He observed that large sell orders of Sandisk and Micron related contracts first appeared on Binance, and then related transactions spread to the stock-linked contract market on Hyperliquid in less than a second.
When the price moves in an unfavorable direction and the account equity falls below the margin level required by the platform, the platform may automatically liquidate the position. For high-leverage long positions, even if the related stocks rebound later, the positions may have already been liquidated.
51.6 million US dollars of positions were forced to liquidate in 10 minutes, which does not represent the total liquidation amount in the US stock market. But it is like a butterfly effect, triggering more fluctuations in the spot market. It can also be said that transactions around the AI industrial chain have extended to the 24/7 leveraged market, and price fluctuations can trigger liquidation before the traditional stock market opens.
03 Short Sellers Make Huge Profits, Retail Investors Buy the Dip
While institutional investors are reducing their holdings in tech stocks, some retail investors are "buying the dip" on stocks in the AI industrial chain.
Capital flow analysis data from Arun Jain, a strategist at JPMorgan Chase, shows that between October 15 and 21, individual investors increased their purchases of chip manufacturers, storage device companies and new cloud computing service providers. The purchase scale of single tech stock rose to the highest level since the market momentum reversed in July, but the purchase intensity of the "Big Seven Tech Stocks" weakened.
On the other side, investors who short companies related to AI infrastructure have obtained considerable paper profits.
On October 22, foreign media cited data from data analysis institution ORTEX and reported that as of that day, investors betting on the share price decline of new US cloud computing companies and data center operators had obtained about 6 billion US dollars of paper profits in the current month. Among the floating shares of companies such as CoreWeave, IREN, Nebius, Applied Digital and Core Scientific, about 20% to 26% are shorted.
Among them, the paper profit of CoreWeave short sellers in this month is close to 1.7 billion US dollars, and the company's share price fell by nearly 30% in the same period. The paper profit of Nebius short sellers in this month is about 2.94 billion US dollars, but the year-to-date figure still records a paper loss of about 3.33 billion US dollars.
It should be noted that the short sellers' profits are concentrated in some AI computing power and data center companies. At the same time, the example of Nebius also shows that the monthly paper profit does not mean that a short selling trade is profitable from beginning to end.
The well-known short seller Chanos' doubts about this kind of company just explain the logic of part of the short selling transactions.
The investor, famous for shorting Enron, revealed in early October that he is shorting most of the new cloud computing companies. Chanos believes that although they are valued by the market as tech growth stocks, their business model is more like a highly leveraged asset leasing business — they buy AI chips and build data centers with borrowed funds, and then lease out computing power to customers.
The risk of this model lies in that enterprises need to invest a large amount of funds to buy chips and build data centers first, and then rely on future computing power lease income to repay the financing cost. If the demand, lease price or equipment utilization rate falls short of expectations, the debt pressure may be amplified.
The overall performance of the US stock market does not mean that all stocks fall at the same time.
In fact, on October 22, nearly two-thirds of the S&P 500 constituent stocks closed up. The reason why the S&P 500 Index still fell by 1.21% is that the index allocates weights according to the market value of companies, and the fall of a few large tech stocks dragged down the index performance.
Statistics from Bespoke Investment Group show that since at least 1990, the S&P 500 Index has only once seen a more significant divergence between positive market breadth and negative index returns — that is, the index is falling, but most constituent stocks are rising.
The last more extreme situation happened in January 2025, when DeepSeek launched a new AI model, triggering the market's doubts about the competitive advantage of large US tech companies and the rationality of their huge capital expenditure.
Next, whether the decline of semiconductor concept stocks can ease, whether institutional position reduction will continue, and whether the financial reports of tech giants such as Microsoft and Amazon can further explain the return on AI investment will be several specific clues to observe market changes.
